124007.e: With protein, around 20 to 30 per cent of the energy taken in is used for processing it. With fat the share is smallest.
124007.m: Protein costs the most energy to process.

124008.q: How does the body quickly produce extra heat using the skeletal muscles when it is cold?
a: By widening the blood vessels in the skin
124008.e: When shivering, the muscles contract rapidly and without coordination. The energy is turned almost completely into heat.
124008.m: Shivering is a quick source of heat in the cold.

124009.q: What is the production of heat in the cold that happens without shivering called?
124009.e: In non-shivering thermogenesis, energy is released directly as heat in the metabolism. It is particularly important in newborn babies.
124009.m: The body can also produce heat without shivering.

124010.q: Which hormones increase the basal metabolic rate and therefore the body's heat production?
124010.e: Thyroxine and triiodothyronine increase the metabolic activity of many cells. People with an overactive thyroid often sweat and hardly feel cold.
124010.m: Thyroid hormones fire up the metabolism.

124011.q: What does the abbreviation NEAT stand for in the energy balance?
a: Energy used in everyday movement without sport
124011.e: NEAT means non-exercise activity thermogenesis. It includes walking, standing, climbing stairs or fidgeting.
124011.m: Everyday movement without sport also uses energy.

124012.q: Why is 2,4-dinitrophenol, which used to be sold as a slimming product, life-threatening?
a: It uncouples the respiratory chain and can cause fatal overheating
It blocks the digestion of fat in the intestine
124012.e: The substance lets protons flow back past ATP synthase. The energy is released as heat instead of as ATP, and body temperature can rise dangerously.
124012.m: Uncouplers turn energy into heat instead of ATP.

124013.q: Which region of the brain controls body temperature and therefore heat production?
124013.e: The body's temperature centre is in the hypothalamus. It compares the actual temperature with the set point and starts heat production or cooling.
124013.m: The hypothalamus is the body's thermostat.

124014.q: Which protein makes heat production possible in brown fat?
124014.e: UCP1 lets protons flow back into the mitochondrial matrix without making ATP. The energy of the gradient is thus turned directly into heat.
124014.m: Thermogenin turns brown fat into a heater.

124015.q: Why is brown fat brownish in colour?
a: It contains a great many mitochondria
It stores a lot of melanin
It contains a lot of bile pigment
It has a poor blood supply
124015.e: The numerous mitochondria contain iron-containing cytochromes. Together with the good blood supply, this produces the brownish colour.
124015.m: The many mitochondria colour brown fat.

124016.q: Where is there a particularly large amount of brown fat in newborn babies?
a: Between the shoulder blades and on the neck
In the soles of the feet
In the lens of the eye
In the bone marrow of the fingers
124016.e: Newborn babies can hardly shiver yet. The brown fat in the back and neck area therefore protects them from getting cold.
124016.m: Newborn babies keep warm with brown fat in the neck.

124017.q: How do brown fat cells differ in structure from white fat cells?
a: They contain many small fat droplets instead of one large one
They contain no fat at all
They are much bigger than white fat cells
124017.e: White fat cells have a single large fat droplet. Brown fat cells are multilocular, so the mitochondria can reach the fatty acids quickly.
124017.m: Brown fat cells have many small fat droplets.

124018.q: Through which part of the nervous system is brown fat activated in the cold?
a: Through the sympathetic nervous system with noradrenaline
Through the parasympathetic nervous system with acetylcholine
Through the motor nerves of the arms
124018.e: Cold stimuli lead to the release of noradrenaline at the brown fat cells. This starts lipolysis and switches on UCP1.
124018.m: In the cold, the sympathetic nervous system switches on brown fat.

124019.q: What are fat cells in white fat called that take on heat-producing properties because of cold?
124019.e: With prolonged cold, cells with UCP1 and many mitochondria can form in white fat. They are called beige or brite fat cells.
124019.m: White fat can partly turn beige and produce heat.

124020.q: Which imaging method made active brown fat in adults visible?
a: A normal X-ray of the lungs
124020.e: Active brown fat takes up a lot of glucose. In PET-CT with labelled glucose it therefore lights up brightly, especially after exposure to cold.
124020.m: Active brown fat shows up in PET-CT.

124021.q: What do hibernating animals such as marmots use their brown fat for in particular?
a: To warm up quickly when they wake
124021.e: When waking from hibernation, the body temperature has to rise a great deal. Brown fat supplies a lot of heat quickly for this.
124021.m: Hibernating animals heat themselves up with brown fat.

124022.q: What is produced from the pyruvate of glycolysis in the alcoholic fermentation of yeast?
124022.e: Without oxygen, yeasts convert pyruvate into ethanol and carbon dioxide. The carbon dioxide makes bread dough rise, for example.
124022.m: Yeast turns pyruvate into ethanol and carbon dioxide.

124023.q: Which organ covers most of its energy needs at rest by breaking down fatty acids?
124023.e: The heart muscle is rich in mitochondria and works non-stop. At rest, most of its ATP comes from beta-oxidation.
124023.m: The heart mainly burns fatty acids.

124024.q: What is the combination of abdominal obesity, high blood pressure, unfavourable blood fats and insulin resistance called?
124024.e: When these risk factors occur together, it is called metabolic syndrome. It clearly increases the risk of heart attack and stroke.
124024.m: Metabolic syndrome combines several metabolic risk factors.

124025.q: Why does the body store energy for the long term mainly as fat rather than as glycogen?
a: Fat is stored without water and is much more energy-dense
Fat can be broken down faster than glycogen
The body cannot store glycogen at all
Fat contains more oxygen than glycogen
124025.e: Glycogen binds a lot of water and supplies little energy per gram of stored weight. Fat is compact and therefore the ideal long-term store.
124025.m: Fat is the body's most compact energy store.

124026.q: Why are the physiological and physical energy values of carbohydrates almost the same?
a: They are broken down completely to carbon dioxide and water in the body
They are not used by the body at all
They contain nitrogen, which is excreted
They do not burn in the calorimeter
124026.e: In the body, as in the calorimeter, carbohydrates end up only as carbon dioxide and water. No waste product containing energy is left over.
124026.m: Nutrients that are broken down completely give the body almost all their energy value.

124027.q: Which substance is formed at the end of the respiratory chain when oxygen takes up electrons and protons?
124027.e: At the last complex of the respiratory chain, oxygen, electrons and protons combine to form water. The carbon dioxide, by contrast, is produced earlier in the citric acid cycle.
124027.m: The respiratory chain turns oxygen into water.

124028.q: Why do many cancer cells use a particularly large amount of glucose?
a: They break down glucose heavily by glycolysis even with oxygen
They need glucose for their cell wall
They pass glucose on to healthy cells
124028.e: Many tumour cells rely heavily on glycolysis and form lactate even when there is enough oxygen. This quickly supplies energy and building blocks for their growth.
124028.m: Cancer cells often rely heavily on glycolysis even with oxygen.

124029.q: How does the basal metabolic rate usually respond to a long and severe reduction in calories?
a: It always stays exactly the same
124029.e: The body adapts to the shortage and saves energy, partly because body mass is lost. This makes further weight loss harder.
124029.m: During strict fasting, the body saves energy.

124030.q: Which SI unit of energy appears on nutrition tables next to the kilocalorie?
124030.e: The joule is the SI unit of energy. On packaging, the energy content is given in kilojoules and in kilocalories.
124030.m: The energy content of food is given in kilojoules.

124031.q: How is the RMS value of an alternating voltage defined?
a: As the DC voltage that converts the same power in a resistor
As the highest value the voltage reaches
As the average voltage over one cycle
As the voltage at the moment of switching on
124031.e: The RMS value compares the heating effect. An alternating voltage with an RMS value of 230 V heats a resistor just as much as 230 V DC.
124031.m: The RMS value equals the DC voltage with the same power.

124032.q: By what factor do you divide the peak value of a sinusoidal voltage to get the RMS value?
124032.e: For sinusoidal quantities, Urms = Umax divided by the square root of 2. The RMS value is therefore about 71 per cent of the peak value.
124032.m: For a sine wave, the RMS value is the peak value divided by the square root of two.

124033.q: A sinusoidal voltage has a peak value of 100 V. What is its RMS value?
124033.m: You get the RMS value of a sine wave by dividing the peak value by 1.414.

124034.q: What is the RMS value of a symmetrical square-wave voltage that jumps between +12 V and -12 V?
124034.e: The voltage has a magnitude of 12 V at every moment. The power in a resistor is therefore the same as with 12 V DC.
124034.m: For a symmetrical square wave the RMS value and the peak value are equal.

124035.q: What is special about a meter labelled “True RMS”?
a: It measures the RMS value correctly even for non-sinusoidal signals
It always shows the peak value
124035.e: Simple meters calculate with a form factor that is only correct for sine waves. True RMS meters work out the real root mean square.
124035.m: A True RMS meter measures the real RMS value of any waveform.

124036.q: What is the arithmetic mean of a sinusoidal voltage over a whole cycle?
124036.e: The positive and negative half-waves are equally large and cancel out. That is why the RMS value is needed for power.
124036.m: The mean of a sinusoidal voltage over one cycle is zero.

124037.q: The mains voltage has an RMS value of 230 V. Roughly what is its peak value?
124037.e: For a sine wave, peak value = RMS value times the square root of 2. 230 V times 1.414 gives about 325 V.
124037.m: The mains voltage reaches peaks of about 325 V.

124038.q: Which mains frequency is usual in the USA?
124038.e: North America uses 60 Hz, Europe 50 Hz. Devices with a clock or a motor must be designed for this.
124038.m: In North America the power grid runs at 60 hertz.

124039.q: Which country has two different mains frequencies, 50 Hz in the east and 60 Hz in the west?
124039.e: In the 19th century eastern and western Japan bought generators from different countries. To this day the grids are linked through frequency converters.

124040.q: What happens to the mains frequency if suddenly more electricity is used than produced?
124040.e: The missing power is taken from the rotational energy of the generators. They slow down and the frequency falls.
124040.m: If power is missing in the grid, the frequency falls.

124041.q: How do power stations in the interconnected grid react within seconds to a falling mains frequency?
124041.e: This automatic reaction is called primary control. Power stations across the whole interconnected grid immediately deliver a little more power until the frequency is stable. Later, secondary and tertiary control take over.
124041.m: Primary control stabilises the frequency within seconds.

124042.q: What is the angular frequency of the 50 Hz grid?
124042.e: ω = 2 × π × f. So 2 × 3.1416 × 50 Hz gives about 314 per second.
124042.m: The angular frequency is two pi times the frequency.

124043.q: Why is the mains frequency the same everywhere in the whole continental European interconnected grid?
a: All the generators turn in sync with each other
Each country measures the frequency again itself
The frequency is sent out by radio
The electricity meters set the frequency
124043.e: The synchronous generators are electrically coupled through the grid. They run in step and form a single synchronous area.
124043.m: An interconnected grid has the same frequency everywhere.

124044.q: In the first moment after a power station fails, what softens the drop in the mains frequency?
a: The inertia of the rotating generators
124044.e: The heavy rotating machines store kinetic energy. This instantaneous reserve is fed into the grid at once.
124044.m: Rotating masses support the mains frequency in the first few seconds.

124045.q: By how many degrees are the three voltages in a three-phase grid out of phase with each other?
124045.e: The three windings in the generator are offset by a third of a circle. That is why the voltages are shifted by 360 ÷ 3 = 120 degrees.
124045.m: The three phases of three-phase current are 120 degrees apart.

124046.q: By what factor is the voltage between two line conductors larger than the voltage between a line conductor and the neutral?
124046.e: Because of the 120-degree phase shift, the difference between two phase voltages is the square root of 3 times as large. 230 V × 1.732 is about 400 V.
124046.m: The line voltage is the square root of three times larger than the phase voltage.

124047.q: How many line conductors does a three-phase grid have?
124047.e: The line conductors are called L1, L2 and L3. There is usually also a neutral conductor and a protective earth conductor.
124047.m: A three-phase grid has three line conductors.

124048.q: How large is the current in the neutral conductor of a star connection when all phases are loaded exactly equally?
124048.e: Three equal currents that are 120 degrees apart always add up to zero. No current flows in the neutral conductor.
124048.m: With a balanced load no current flows in the neutral conductor.

124049.q: What are the two basic connections of three-phase loads called?
124049.e: In a star, each phase winding lies between a line conductor and the star point; in a delta, between two line conductors. The windings therefore get different voltages.
124049.m: Three-phase loads are connected in star or in delta.

124050.q: Which property makes three-phase current especially suitable for electric motors?
a: It produces a rotating magnetic field in three coils
It has a higher frequency than alternating current
It only flows in one direction
124050.e: Three offset coils with offset currents produce a magnetic field that rotates. This rotating field pulls the rotor round with it.
124050.m: Three-phase current produces a rotating field that drives motors.

124051.q: What real power does a balanced three-phase load take with a line voltage of 400 V, a line current of 10 A and cos phi = 1?
124051.e: P = √3 × U × I × cos phi = 1.732 × 400 V × 10 A × 1, which gives about 6928 W.
124051.m: Three-phase power is calculated with the factor of the square root of three.

124052.q: Which Swiss company took part in the first long-distance transmission of three-phase current from Lauffen am Neckar to Frankfurt in 1891?
124052.e: AEG and Maschinenfabrik Oerlikon supplied the system for the electrical exhibition in Frankfurt. The line was about 175 km long.
124052.m: The first long-distance three-phase transmission was built with Swiss involvement.

124053.q: What is characteristic of a synchronous motor?
a: The rotor turns at exactly the speed of the rotating field
The rotor always turns a little more slowly than the rotating field
The rotor turns twice as fast as the rotating field
The rotor needs no magnetic field
124053.e: The magnetised rotor is carried along by the rotating field like a compass needle. It therefore runs in step, that is synchronously.
124053.m: A synchronous motor turns in step with the rotating field.

124054.q: At what speed does a synchronous motor with two pole pairs run on the 50 Hz mains?
124054.e: n = 60 × f ÷ p = 60 × 50 ÷ 2 = 1500 revolutions per minute.
124054.m: The speed of a synchronous motor depends on the frequency and the number of pole pairs.

124055.q: What is the speed of the rotating field of a machine with one pole pair on the 50 Hz mains?
124055.e: With one pole pair, the field makes one revolution per mains cycle, so 50 per second. That is 50 × 60 = 3000 per minute.
124055.m: With one pole pair the field turns fifty times a second.

124056.q: Why does a simple synchronous motor connected to a fixed grid not start by itself?
a: The heavy rotor cannot follow the fast rotating field from a standstill
It has no windings in the stator
It only works with direct current
124056.e: The rotating field changes direction so quickly that the stationary rotor is only pulled back and forth. A starting aid or a frequency converter is needed.
124056.m: A synchronous motor needs help to start.

124057.q: How is the rotor of a synchronous motor magnetised?
a: By permanent magnets or a winding excited with direct current
Only by induction from the rotating field
124057.e: The rotor needs its own fixed magnetic field. This is provided by permanent magnets or an exciter winding with direct current.
124057.m: The rotor of a synchronous motor has its own magnetic field.

124058.q: Which machine is fitted as the generator in most large power stations?
124058.e: The speed of the synchronous machine is firmly linked to the mains frequency. That is why hydroelectric and nuclear power stations mostly produce their electricity with synchronous generators.
124058.m: Power station generators are mostly synchronous machines.

124059.q: What must match before a synchronous generator in a power station is connected to the grid?
a: Voltage, frequency and phase must match the grid
The generator must be at a standstill
The generator must turn twice as fast as the grid
The generator must deliver direct current
124059.e: During synchronisation, voltage, frequency and phase are matched. Otherwise large equalising currents would flow when connecting.
124059.m: A generator is only connected once it is in step with the grid.

124060.q: Why do clocks with a small synchronous motor keep accurate time as long as the mains frequency is right?
a: Their speed is firmly linked to the mains frequency
They do not count the voltage peaks
124060.e: The synchronous motor turns exactly in step with the mains frequency. That is why grid operators even out frequency deviations over the course of the day.
124060.m: Synchronous clocks count the oscillations of the grid.

124061.q: What happens if a synchronous motor is loaded too heavily?
a: It falls out of step and stops
It turns faster than the rotating field
124061.e: If the load torque exceeds the pull-out torque, the rotor can no longer follow the field. It loses synchronism and must be switched off.
124061.m: When overloaded, the synchronous motor loses synchronism.

124062.q: What is called slip in an induction motor?
a: The relative difference between the speed of the rotating field and the rotor
124062.e: Slip is (n_field minus n_rotor) ÷ n_field. It is usually given in per cent.
124062.m: Slip describes how much more slowly the rotor turns than the rotating field.

124063.q: A rotating field turns at 1500 per minute and the rotor at 1440 per minute. What is the slip?
124063.m: Slip is the difference in speed divided by the speed of the field.

124064.q: What is the most common type of rotor in an induction motor called?
124064.e: The rotor consists of aluminium or copper bars short-circuited at the ends by rings. It looks like a hamster wheel.
124064.m: The squirrel-cage rotor is robust and needs no sliding contacts.

124065.q: Why can the rotor of an induction motor never quite reach the speed of the rotating field?
a: Without a difference in speed no current would be induced in the rotor
Because the friction in the bearing is too great
Because the rotor is made of plastic
124065.e: Induction only occurs if the field moves relative to the rotor. Without rotor current there would be no torque.
124065.m: An induction motor needs slip to produce torque.

124066.q: What in the stator of a three-phase induction motor produces the turning of the rotor?
a: A rotating magnetic field from three currents out of phase
A permanent magnet that turns along with it
An electrostatic field between two plates
124066.e: Alternating currents shifted in time flow through the three windings in the stator. This creates a rotating magnetic field that induces currents in the rotor and pulls it along.
124066.m: The rotating field in the stator drives the induction motor.

124067.q: What is star-delta starting used for in larger induction motors?
a: It lowers the high starting current
It reverses the direction of rotation
124067.e: When starting in star connection, each winding only gets the phase voltage. The starting current falls to about a third, and then the motor is switched to delta.
124067.m: Star-delta starting protects the grid when switching on.

124068.q: How do you reverse the direction of rotation of a three-phase induction motor?
a: Swap the neutral and earth conductors
124068.e: Swapping two phases changes the order of the voltages. The rotating field, and with it the motor, then runs the other way.
124068.m: Swapping two line conductors reverses the direction of rotation.

124069.q: Which device can adjust the speed of an induction motor smoothly?
124069.e: The frequency converter produces a voltage with a variable frequency. This changes the speed of the rotating field and the motor.
124069.m: A frequency converter controls the speed through the frequency.

124070.q: How large is the starting current of an induction motor switched on directly, typically?
a: About five to eight times the rated current
Exactly the same as the rated current
About a hundred times the rated current
124070.e: At a standstill the slip is at its maximum and a very high current is induced in the rotor. The current only falls as the speed rises.
124070.m: Induction motors draw several times their rated current when switched on.

124071.q: The transmission voltage is increased tenfold for the same power. How do the line losses change?
124071.e: The current falls to a tenth. Because the losses grow with I², they fall to (1/10)² = 1/100.
124071.m: Line losses decrease with the square of the current.

124072.q: At what frequency does a transformer on the 50 Hz mains mainly hum?
124072.e: Through magnetostriction, the sheets change length at every peak of magnetisation, whatever its direction. That happens twice per cycle.
124072.m: A transformer on the 50 Hz mains hums at 100 hertz.

124073.q: Roughly what efficiency do large power transformers achieve?
124073.e: Large transformers have no moving parts and very well optimised cores. Their losses are below one per cent.
124073.m: Large transformers work almost without losses.

124074.q: An ideal transformer converts 230 V and 1 A on the primary side into 23 V. What current flows on the secondary side?
124074.e: In an ideal transformer the power stays the same: 230 V × 1 A = 230 W. This gives I = 230 W ÷ 23 V = 10 A.
124074.m: If the voltage is lowered, the current rises in the same ratio.

124075.q: What is special about an autotransformer?
a: The primary and secondary sides share a common winding
It has no iron core at all
124075.e: In an autotransformer the secondary voltage is taken from a tap on the winding. This saves copper but does not separate the circuits.
124075.m: An autotransformer manages with a single winding.

124076.q: What is an isolating transformer for?
a: It isolates the circuit electrically from the mains
It turns alternating current into direct current
It stores energy for power cuts
124076.e: There is no conducting connection between the primary and secondary windings. Anyone touching a conductor does not form a circuit to earth, which increases safety.
124076.m: An isolating transformer protects through electrical isolation.

124077.q: What are large power transformers in substations usually cooled and insulated with?
124077.e: The windings sit in a tank of insulating oil. The oil carries the heat to the cooling fins and insulates at the same time.
124077.m: Large transformers stand in an oil bath.

124078.q: What advantage does HVDC offer when connecting two grids?
a: It can link grids with different frequencies or not in sync
It increases the frequency of both grids
It only works within one grid
124078.e: The DC link decouples the two AC grids. They therefore do not have to run in sync.
124078.m: HVDC can even connect grids that do not run in step.

124079.q: Which semiconductor components are used in modern HVDC converter stations?
124079.e: Older systems use thyristors, newer ones mainly IGBTs. They switch very large currents and voltages.
124079.m: HVDC stations work with high-power semiconductors.

124080.q: To which island did the world's first commercial HVDC link lead?
124080.e: The Swedish company ASEA connected the island of Gotland to the mainland with an undersea cable. This was the start of commercial HVDC technology.
124080.m: The first commercial HVDC link led to Gotland.

124081.q: What is the main disadvantage of HVDC?
a: The lines must be made of gold
124081.e: Complex converters are needed at both ends. That is why HVDC only pays off over large distances, for undersea cables or for linking grids.
124081.m: Because of the expensive stations, HVDC only pays off over long distances.

124082.q: How many conductors does a bipolar HVDC link need?
124082.e: One conductor carries a positive and the other a negative voltage relative to earth. Three-phase current, by contrast, needs three conductors.
124082.m: A bipolar HVDC line manages with two conductors.

124083.q: What does the converter station at the receiving end of an HVDC line do?
a: It turns direct current back into alternating current
It turns alternating current into direct current
It stores the electricity in batteries
124083.e: There the station works as an inverter and feeds alternating current into the grid. The rectifier is at the start of the line.
124083.m: At the end of an HVDC link alternating current is produced again.

124084.q: Which effect, which pushes alternating current to the surface of a conductor, plays no role in HVDC?
124084.e: With direct current the current spreads evenly over the whole cross-section. The conductor is therefore used better.
124084.m: Direct current uses the whole cross-section of the conductor.

124085.q: Why are HVDC systems built with the rectifier and inverter at the same place, with no long-distance line at all?
a: To link two neighbouring grids that do not run in step
To transmit electricity over long distances
124085.e: Such a back-to-back link connects two neighbouring AC grids. The DC section is only a few metres long and decouples the grids.
124085.m: An HVDC back-to-back link connects neighbouring grids.

124086.q: Besides operating the lines, what job does Swissgrid have?
a: It keeps generation and consumption in balance
124086.e: Swissgrid obtains balancing power and so keeps the mains frequency stable. Selling electricity is done by the energy suppliers.
124086.m: Swissgrid keeps the Swiss grid in balance.

124087.q: Which federal law required an independent national grid company for the transmission grid?
124087.e: The Electricity Supply Act governs the opening of the electricity market. It states that the transmission grid must be run by an independent company.
124087.m: The Electricity Supply Act is the basis for Swissgrid.

124088.q: According to the law, who must own the majority of Swissgrid?
a: Cantons and municipalities, directly or indirectly
124088.e: The Electricity Supply Act requires the majority of capital and voting rights to lie with cantons and municipalities, either directly or through their energy companies.
124088.m: Swissgrid is mostly owned by the Swiss public sector.

124089.q: In which association does Swissgrid work together with the other European transmission system operators?
124089.e: In the ENTSO-E association, Europe's transmission system operators coordinate planning and operation. Swissgrid is a member.
124089.m: Swissgrid is part of the European association of grid operators.

124090.q: Which grid level is Swissgrid's transmission grid in Switzerland?
124090.e: The Swiss power grid is divided into seven grid levels. Extra-high voltage forms grid level 1, and households are connected to grid level 7.
124090.m: The transmission grid is the top grid level.

124091.q: Which independent authority in Switzerland supervises grid usage charges and therefore Swissgrid too?
a: The Financial Market Supervisory Authority FINMA
124091.e: ElCom is the regulatory authority for electricity. Among other things it checks grid tariffs and the security of supply.
124091.m: ElCom regulates the Swiss electricity market.

124092.q: How are the costs of Swissgrid's transmission grid mainly paid for?
a: Through grid usage charges on the electricity bill
124092.e: The costs are passed on through grid tariffs to the distribution system operators and finally to the end customers. They are part of the price of electricity.
124092.m: The transmission grid is paid for through the electricity bill.

124093.q: In which unit is reactive power given?
124093.e: The unit var stands for volt-ampere reactive. It distinguishes reactive power from real power in watts.
124093.m: Reactive power is given in var.

124094.q: A load has a real power of 3 kW and a reactive power of 4 kvar. What is the apparent power?
124094.e: S = square root of (P² + Q²) = square root of (9 + 16) = square root of 25 = 5 kVA.
124094.m: Apparent, real and reactive power form a right-angled triangle.

124095.q: What is the power factor cos phi with a real power of 8 kW and an apparent power of 10 kVA?
124095.e: cos phi = P ÷ S = 8 kW ÷ 10 kVA = 0.8.
124095.m: The power factor is real power divided by apparent power.

124096.q: Which components cause reactive power in AC circuits?
124096.e: In coils and capacitors energy is stored in fields and given back again. Current and voltage are shifted relative to each other.
124096.m: Coils and capacitors swing reactive power back and forth.

124097.q: What is used to compensate for the inductive reactive power of large motors?
124097.e: Capacitors take up reactive power with the opposite sign. In this way the reactive currents largely cancel out.
124097.m: Capacitors balance out inductive reactive power.

124098.q: How does the current in an ideal coil behave compared with the voltage?
a: It lags the voltage by 90 degrees
It leads the voltage by 90 degrees
It is in phase with the voltage
124098.e: Through self-induction the coil resists every change in current. That is why the current only reaches its maximum a quarter of a cycle after the voltage.
124098.m: In a coil the current comes late.

124099.q: How does the current in an ideal capacitor behave compared with the voltage?
a: It leads the voltage by 90 degrees
It lags the voltage by 90 degrees
It is in phase with the voltage
124099.e: The capacitor must first be charged before there is a voltage across it. The charging current is greatest when the voltage passes through zero.
124099.m: In a capacitor the current leads.

124100.q: Why is a lot of reactive power in the grid unwanted?
a: It loads the lines with current without doing useful work
124100.e: Reactive currents flow back and forth and heat the lines. Lines and transformers have to be built larger to cope.
124100.m: Reactive power loads the grid without any benefit.

124101.q: In which unit is apparent power given?
124101.e: Apparent power is the product of RMS voltage and RMS current. Its unit is the volt-ampere.
124101.m: Apparent power is given in volt-amperes.

124102.q: Between which forms of energy does the energy swing back and forth in an electrical oscillating circuit?
a: The electric field of the capacitor and the magnetic field of the coil
124102.e: The charged capacitor discharges through the coil and builds up a magnetic field. This collapses and charges the capacitor again the other way round.
124102.m: In an oscillating circuit the energy alternates between capacitor and coil.

124103.q: How does the natural frequency of an oscillating circuit change if you quadruple the capacitance?
124103.e: The frequency is inversely proportional to the square root of C. The square root of 4 is 2, so the frequency falls to half.
124103.m: Four times the capacitance means half the frequency.

124104.q: Why does the oscillation in a real oscillating circuit gradually die away?
a: The ohmic resistance turns energy into heat
124104.e: With every swing back and forth, energy is lost as heat in the wires. The amplitude therefore decreases; this is called damping.

124105.q: What is an adjustable oscillating circuit used for in a classic radio receiver?
124105.e: A variable capacitor changes the natural frequency of the circuit. It then responds strongly only to the station with that frequency.
124105.m: An oscillating circuit selects the station you want on the radio.

124106.q: How does the impedance of a series oscillating circuit behave at its resonant frequency?
a: It is at its minimum and equals the ohmic resistance
It is zero ohms, even with losses
It is the same as at any other frequency
124106.e: At resonance the reactances of the coil and the capacitor cancel out. Only the ohmic part remains.
124106.m: At resonance a series circuit lets the most current through.

124107.q: How does the impedance of an ideal parallel oscillating circuit behave at resonance?
a: It equals exactly the resistance of the coil
124107.e: In the parallel circuit at resonance the current only swings between the coil and the capacitor. Hardly any current flows in from outside, so the circuit blocks.
124107.m: A parallel oscillating circuit blocks at its resonant frequency.

124108.q: How can the oscillation in an oscillating circuit be kept going permanently?
a: Through feedback that supplies energy in the right rhythm
By charging it more strongly once
124108.e: A real oscillating circuit loses energy with every oscillation. A feedback circuit with an amplifier supplies this energy again in time with the oscillation.
124108.m: Feedback cancels out the damping of an oscillation.

124109.q: At what speed do electromagnetic waves travel in a vacuum?
124109.e: All electromagnetic waves travel at the speed of light in a vacuum. It is almost exactly 300,000 km per second.
124109.m: Electromagnetic waves are as fast as light.

124110.q: How are the electric and magnetic fields arranged in an electromagnetic wave?
a: At right angles to each other and to the direction of travel
Parallel to each other and to the direction of travel
Both along the direction of travel
124110.e: Electromagnetic waves are transverse waves. The two fields oscillate across the direction of travel and are perpendicular to each other.

124111.q: Which physicist predicted the existence of electromagnetic waves in theory with his equations?
124111.e: Maxwell summed up electricity and magnetism in four equations. From these followed waves that travel at the speed of light.
124111.m: Maxwell predicted electromagnetic waves in theory.

124112.q: What distinguishes electromagnetic waves from sound waves?
a: They need no medium and also travel through a vacuum
124112.e: The fields create each other and need no carrier. That is why sunlight reaches us through empty space.
124112.m: Electromagnetic waves can cross a vacuum too.

124113.q: Which kind of electromagnetic radiation has the highest frequency?
124113.e: The spectrum ranges from radio waves through microwaves, infrared, light and ultraviolet to X-rays and gamma rays. Gamma radiation has the most energy.
124113.m: Gamma radiation has the highest frequency in the spectrum.

124114.q: How long is a simple dipole antenna tuned to a wave, compared with the wavelength?
124114.e: In a half-wave dipole a standing wave forms with a current maximum in the middle. That is why it radiates especially well.
124114.m: A dipole antenna is usually half a wavelength long.

124115.q: At which university did Heinrich Hertz carry out his famous experiments with electromagnetic waves?
124115.e: Hertz was a professor in Karlsruhe when he carried out his experiments there. Afterwards he moved to Bonn.
124115.m: Heinrich Hertz did his research in Karlsruhe.

124116.q: What did Hertz use to produce electromagnetic waves in his experiments?
124116.e: An induction coil produced a high voltage across a spark gap. The rapid discharges gave off waves, which Hertz detected with a receiving loop.
124116.m: Hertz produced waves with electric sparks.

124117.q: What did Hertz discover along the way during his spark experiments?
a: That ultraviolet light makes it easier for sparks to jump
124117.e: Hertz observed that UV light helps sparks to form. This was an early sign of the photoelectric effect.
124117.m: Hertz was an early observer of the photoelectric effect.

124118.q: In which city was Heinrich Hertz born?
124118.e: Heinrich Rudolf Hertz was born in Hamburg. There, among other things, the Heinrich Hertz Tower reminds people of him.

124119.q: How old was Heinrich Hertz when he died?
124119.e: Hertz died after a serious illness in early 1894 in Bonn. He was only 36 years old.

124120.q: Under which famous physicist did Heinrich Hertz study in Berlin?
124120.e: Helmholtz supported Hertz and encouraged him to study fast electrical oscillations.
124120.m: Heinrich Hertz was a student of Hermann von Helmholtz.

124121.q: Which relative of Heinrich Hertz later won the Nobel Prize in Physics?
124121.e: Gustav Hertz was honoured together with James Franck for the Franck-Hertz experiment. The experiment confirmed separate energy levels in atoms.
124121.m: Gustav Hertz was also an important physicist.

124122.q: A 46 ohm heating resistor is connected to an alternating voltage with an RMS value of 230 V. What power does it convert?
124122.e: With the RMS value you calculate as with DC voltage: P = U² ÷ R = 230 V × 230 V ÷ 46 ohms = 1150 W.
124122.m: With the RMS value, power can be calculated as for direct current.

124123.q: Which emergency measure is triggered automatically when the mains frequency drops sharply, to prevent a widespread power cut?
a: An increase in the mains voltage
124123.e: If the reserves are not enough, groups of consumers are automatically disconnected from the grid. This allows the balance to be restored.
124123.m: When the frequency drops sharply, consumers are deliberately switched off.

124124.q: What does a transformer draw when nothing is connected to its secondary side?
a: Only a small no-load current for magnetisation
No current at all, not even a magnetising current
124124.e: With no load, the primary winding acts like a coil with a large reactance. Only a small current flows, which magnetises the core and covers the iron losses.
124124.m: An unloaded transformer needs only a little current.

124125.q: What does the (n-1) criterion require when operating the transmission grid?
a: The grid must cope with the failure of any single element without interrupting supply
A power station may never feed more than one line
There may only be one line per canton
Every line is switched off once a year
124125.e: If a line or a transformer fails, the remaining equipment must be able to take over the load. This keeps the supply secure.
124125.m: The grid must be able to cope with any single failure.

124126.q: What does the quality factor of an oscillating circuit tell you?
a: How weakly it is damped and how sharp its resonance is
How high its operating voltage may be
How many turns the coil has
124126.e: A circuit with a high quality factor loses little energy per oscillation. Its resonance curve is narrow and tall.
124126.m: A high quality factor means little damping and sharp resonance.

124127.q: Roughly what wavelength does a 900 MHz mobile phone signal have?
124127.m: The higher the frequency, the shorter the wavelength.

124128.q: What does an electromagnetic wave carry, for example the light from the Sun to the Earth?
124128.e: Electromagnetic waves carry energy through space, even through a vacuum. No matter is carried along.

124129.q: Which inventor used the waves studied by Hertz shortly afterwards for wireless telegraphy?
124129.e: Marconi built on Hertz’s findings and transmitted signals over ever greater distances. This developed into radio.
124129.m: Marconi turned Hertzian waves into radio technology.

124130.e: Pharmacognosy is the study of medicinal substances from living things, that is from plants, fungi, animals or microorganisms. It is a classic subject in pharmacy degrees.
124130.m: Pharmacognosy studies medicinal substances from nature.

124131.q: In pharmacognosy, what are dried plant parts called that serve as the starting material for medicines?
124131.e: In pharmacy, “drug” originally simply meant a dried natural raw material. The word probably comes from the Dutch “droog”, meaning dry.
124131.m: A crude drug is a dried plant part.

124132.q: Which Latin term means the root in the names of crude drugs?
124132.e: Radix means root, folium leaf, cortex bark and semen seed. For example, valerian root is called “Valerianae radix”.
124132.m: Radix is the Latin name for root.

124133.q: What is a herbal tea called for which boiling water is poured over the crude drug and left to steep?
124133.e: For an infusion, boiling water is poured over the crude drug. A decoction, by contrast, is boiled, and a macerate is made with cold water.
124133.m: An infusion is made by pouring hot water over the plant.

124134.q: What is a preparation called in which a hard crude drug such as bark or root is boiled in water?
124134.e: Hard plant parts release their substances poorly when hot water is just poured over them. That is why they are prepared by boiling, in Latin a decoction.
124134.m: A decoction is made by boiling.

124135.q: In pharmacy, what is a tincture?
a: An extract of a crude drug made with ethanol
124135.e: Tinctures are liquid extracts, usually made with a mixture of ethanol and water. Alcohol dissolves many substances well and makes the extract keep.
124135.m: A tincture is an alcoholic plant extract.

124136.q: In Switzerland, which work, together with the Pharmacopoea Helvetica, sets out the quality requirements for crude drugs?
124136.e: Switzerland applies the European Pharmacopoeia (Pharmacopoea Europaea). The Pharmacopoea Helvetica adds national rules to it.
124136.m: The pharmacopoeia sets out what good crude drugs must be like.

124137.q: What is treating illnesses with plants, plant parts and preparations made from them called?
124137.e: The Greek “phyton” means plant. Phytotherapy uses herbal medicines whose effect is based on the substances they contain.

124138.q: What distinguishes secondary plant substances from products of primary metabolism?
a: They are not directly needed for growth and energy production
They are only made at night
124138.e: Every cell needs primary substances such as sugars, amino acids and fats to live. Secondary substances carry out special tasks such as defence, attraction or protection.
124138.m: Secondary plant substances do not serve basic metabolism but special tasks.

124139.q: Which task do many secondary plant substances carry out for the plant?
a: Building the cell wall from cellulose
124139.e: Many secondary substances are bitter, poisonous or antimicrobial. Plants, which cannot run away, use them to protect themselves from animals, fungi and bacteria.

124140.q: What is the group of natural substances containing nitrogen, usually basic, called, to which caffeine and nicotine belong?
124140.e: Alkaloids contain nitrogen, usually in a ring, and often react as bases. Many of them have a strong effect on the nervous system.
124140.m: Alkaloids are plant substances containing nitrogen.

124141.q: Glucosinolates, which release hot mustard oils when chewed, are typical of which plant family?
124141.e: Mustard, cabbage, radish and cress belong to the crucifers. When the tissue is damaged, the enzyme myrosinase splits the glucosinolates into hot mustard oils.
124141.m: Cabbage and mustard protect themselves with mustard oils.

124142.q: Which substance makes chilli peppers hot?
124142.e: Capsaicin stimulates heat and pain receptors (TRPV1) and so produces the burning feeling. Piperine, on the other hand, makes black pepper hot.

124143.q: How can you recognise saponins when you shake a plant solution with water?
124143.e: Saponins are soap-like glycosides that lower surface tension. The name comes from the Latin “sapo”, meaning soap.

124144.q: Which poisonous gas can cyanogenic glycosides such as amygdalin from bitter almonds release?
124144.e: Amygdalin is split by enzymes, producing hydrogen cyanide (prussic acid). That is why larger amounts of bitter almonds are poisonous.
124144.m: Bitter almonds can release hydrogen cyanide.

124145.q: Which secondary plant substance is produced by the grapevine when a fungus attacks the plant?
124145.e: Resveratrol inhibits fungi and is produced in greater amounts by the vine after an infection. It also occurs in grape skins and red wine.
124145.m: Among other things, the grapevine fights off fungi with resveratrol.

124146.q: From which basic building blocks are terpenes formally built?
a: From isoprene units with 5 carbon atoms
124146.e: Terpenes can be described as several isoprene units (C5H8) joined together. This rule is called the isoprene rule.
124146.m: Terpenes are made of isoprene building blocks.

124147.q: How many carbon atoms does the basic skeleton of a monoterpene have?
124147.e: A monoterpene consists of two isoprene units of 5 carbon atoms each. 2 times 5 gives 10 carbon atoms.

124148.q: What are terpenes with 15 carbon atoms called?
124148.e: “Sesqui” means one and a half: one and a half monoterpenes, that is three isoprene units of 5 carbon atoms. That gives 15 carbon atoms.

124149.q: Which natural substance is a polyterpene made of very many isoprene units?
124149.e: The milky sap of the rubber tree contains cis-polyisoprene. Natural rubber is made from it.

124150.q: Which class of terpenes does beta-carotene, with 40 carbon atoms, belong to?
124150.e: 40 carbon atoms correspond to eight isoprene units or four monoterpene units. That is why carotenoids count as tetraterpenes.

124151.q: Which terpene gives peppermint its cooling taste?
124151.e: Menthol is a monoterpene alcohol from peppermint oil. It stimulates the cold receptors of the skin and therefore feels cooling.
124151.m: Menthol from peppermint is a terpene.

124152.q: What do many terpenes do for plants?
a: They act as scents and defensive substances
They are building material for the cell wall
124152.e: Many terpenes smell strongly, scare off herbivores or attract pollinators. Essential oils from mint or conifers contain many terpenes.
124152.m: Terpenes often serve plants as scents and defensive substances.

124153.q: Which solvent is distilled from the resin of pine trees and consists mainly of monoterpenes such as pinene?
124153.e: Distilling pine resin produces turpentine, and rosin is left behind. The word “terpene” comes from turpentine.

124154.q: Where does the name “flavonoids” come from?
a: From the name of a chemist
124154.e: Many flavonoids are yellow plant pigments. That is why the group was named after the Latin word for yellow.
124154.m: Flavonoids are named after the colour yellow.

124155.q: What job do flavonoids do in the leaves of many plants?
a: They anchor the plant in the soil
They carry sugar to the roots
124155.e: Flavonoids in the outer layers of the leaf absorb UV light. In this way they protect the genetic material and the photosynthesis machinery of the cells.
124155.m: In leaves, flavonoids work like a sunscreen.

124156.q: Which flavonoids colour many flowers and fruits red, purple or blue?
124156.e: Anthocyanins are water-soluble pigments in the vacuole. They colour cherries, blueberries and red cabbage, for example.
124156.m: Anthocyanins colour plants red to blue.

124157.q: Why can red cabbage juice be used as an acid-base indicator?
a: Its anthocyanins change colour with the pH
It only conducts electricity in acids
124157.e: The structure of anthocyanins changes depending on the pH, and so does their colour. In acid the juice turns red, in alkali green to yellow.
124157.m: Red cabbage juice shows the pH with its colour.

124158.q: Which flavonol is found in particularly large amounts in onions, especially in the skins?
124158.e: Quercetin is one of the most common flavonols in food. Because of pigments like this, onion skins dye Easter eggs yellowish brown.

124159.q: In which legume are isoflavones such as genistein found in particularly large amounts?
124159.e: Isoflavones occur almost only in legumes, most of all in the soya bean. They are also called phytoestrogens.
124159.m: The soya bean contains a lot of isoflavones.

124160.q: What are the coloured flavonoids in many flowers for?
124160.e: Pigments such as anthocyanins make flowers visible to insects and birds. Some flavonoids also form UV patterns that bees can see but people cannot.
124160.m: Flavonoids make flowers stand out to pollinators.

124161.q: Which flavonoids are found in particularly large amounts in green tea?
124161.e: Green tea contains many catechins such as epigallocatechin gallate. When it is fermented into black tea, most of them are turned into theaflavins.
124161.m: Green tea is rich in catechins.

124162.q: How did tannins get their name?
a: They were used to tan animal hides into leather
124162.e: Tannins link up the proteins of the hide, which then becomes durable leather. In the past, oak and spruce bark were mainly used for this.
124162.m: Tannins are used to turn hide into leather.

124163.q: What effect do tannins have on skin and mucous membranes?
124163.e: Tannins bind proteins in the top layers of cells and make them denser. This creates a protective layer, and the mucous membrane tightens.

124164.q: What causes the furry feeling in the mouth after unripe fruit or strong black tea?
a: Tannins bind proteins in the saliva and on the mucous membrane
124164.e: Tannins make the proteins in saliva clump together, so it no longer lubricates well. This feels dry and furry.
124164.m: Tannins make your mouth feel furry.

124165.q: Why does red wine usually taste drier and harsher than white wine?
a: It contains more tannins from skins and seeds
It is stored at a lower temperature
124165.e: For red wine, the juice ferments together with the skins and seeds. Many tannins pass into the wine, giving it a harsh, furry feel.
124165.m: Red wine contains many tannins from the grape skins.

124166.q: What job do tannins do for the plant itself?
a: They protect against herbivores and pathogens
They store energy for the winter
124166.e: Tannins taste harsh and bind proteins, including the digestive enzymes of animals and the enzymes of fungi. That is why many animals avoid plant parts rich in tannins.
124166.m: Tannins protect plants from being eaten.

124167.q: Which bark is a classic tannin-rich crude drug of European folk medicine, used for example for sitz baths and compresses?
124167.e: Oak bark contains plenty of tannins and is used externally for mild skin inflammation. It was also used in the past for tanning leather with bark.
124167.m: Oak bark is rich in tannins.

124168.q: Which ink used to be made from tannin-rich oak galls and iron salts?
124168.e: Oak galls are growths on oak leaves caused by gall wasps. Their tannins form a dark, long-lasting ink with iron salts.
124168.m: Iron gall ink is made from oak galls and iron.

124169.q: Which dried berries are traditionally used for mild diarrhoea because of their tannins?
124169.e: Dried bilberries contain tannins that have an astringent effect on the lining of the gut. Fresh bilberries are not suitable for this.
124169.m: Dried bilberries are a traditional remedy for mild diarrhoea.

124170.q: By which process are most essential oils obtained from plants?
124170.e: Hot steam carries the volatile scent substances with it. After cooling, the oil separates from the water.
124170.m: Essential oils are usually obtained by steam distillation.

124171.q: How are essential oils from citrus peel usually obtained?
124171.e: The oils are in oil glands just under the surface of the peel. Pressing mechanically without heat leaves the scent substances unchanged.

124172.q: How can you tell an essential oil from a fatty oil on paper?
a: It evaporates and leaves no lasting grease mark
It sets the paper on fire immediately
124172.e: Essential oils are volatile and evaporate completely. Fatty oils such as olive oil do not evaporate and leave a see-through mark.
124172.m: Essential oils evaporate without a trace.

124173.q: What is scented plant water such as rose water called, which is produced alongside the essential oil during steam distillation?
124173.e: The hydrosol contains small amounts of dissolved scent substances. Well-known examples are rose water and orange blossom water.
124173.m: The hydrosol is the scented water from distillation.

124174.q: In which structures do members of the mint family such as peppermint and sage store their essential oil?
a: In glandular hairs on the leaf surface
In the vessels of the wood
124174.e: Members of the mint family have glandular scales in which the oil collects under a cuticle. If you rub the leaf, they burst and give off a scent.
124174.m: Plants of the mint family store oil in glandular hairs.

124175.q: What has clove oil long been used for in dentistry?
a: Against toothache, because it numbs locally
Against tooth decay, because it contains fluoride
124175.e: Clove oil contains a lot of eugenol. This substance numbs locally and is antiseptic, so it is used for toothache and in dental cements.

124176.q: Which substance gives thyme oil its strong antiseptic effect?
124176.e: Thymol is a phenol from the group of monoterpenes and works against bacteria and fungi. That is why thyme is used in cough medicines.

124177.q: What is chamomile mainly used for in folk medicine?
a: Against inflammation, for example as tea or a steam bath
As a remedy for broken bones
124177.e: Chamomile flowers contain an essential oil with anti-inflammatory substances. That is why chamomile tea, rinses and steam baths are used for inflammation.

124178.q: What is eucalyptus oil often used for?
a: For inhaling when you have a cold
As a substitute for cooking oil when frying
124178.e: Eucalyptus oil contains mainly cineole, which clears the airways. That is why it is inhaled for colds or used in chest rubs.
124178.m: Inhaling eucalyptus oil helps against colds.

124179.q: Which Latin plant name does the name “salicylic acid” come from?
124179.e: In willow bark, the precursor salicin was found, from which salicylic acid is formed. Salix is the Latin genus name of the willows.
124179.m: Salicylic acid is named after the willow.

124180.q: What is the precursor in willow bark called that is turned into salicylic acid in the body?
124180.e: Salicin is a glycoside. In the gut and liver it is converted into salicyl alcohol and then into salicylic acid.

124181.q: Which group of medicines does acetylsalicylic acid belong to?
124181.e: Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs relieve pain, reduce fever and reduce inflammation without having a cortisone structure. Ibuprofen and diclofenac belong to the same group.
124181.m: Acetylsalicylic acid is a non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug.

124182.q: Why is low-dose acetylsalicylic acid prescribed to prevent heart attacks?
a: It stops blood platelets from clumping together
124182.e: In the blood platelets, the substance blocks the production of thromboxane, which encourages clumping. Because platelets have no nucleus, the effect lasts their whole lifetime.
124182.m: A little aspirin inhibits the blood platelets.

124183.q: How does acetylsalicylic acid work against pain and inflammation?
a: It blocks cyclooxygenase and so the production of prostaglandins
It blocks the sodium channels of nerves
124183.e: Acetylsalicylic acid transfers an acetyl group to the enzyme cyclooxygenase and blocks it permanently. As a result fewer prostaglandins, which pass on pain and inflammation, are produced.

124184.q: What is salicylic acid used for in skin products such as wart plasters?
124184.e: Salicylic acid is keratolytic: it loosens the bonds between horny skin cells. This makes it possible to remove calluses, corns and warts.

124185.q: What role does salicylic acid play in the plant itself?
a: It is a signal substance for defence against pathogens
It is the most important storage sugar
124185.e: After an infection, the salicylic acid level rises and switches on defence genes. In this way the whole plant can become more resistant (systemic acquired resistance).
124185.m: Salicylic acid is a defence signal in the plant.

124186.q: Why are children and teenagers with viral infections usually not given acetylsalicylic acid?
a: Because of the risk of Reye's syndrome
Because it does not work in children
124186.e: In children with viral infections, a link with the rare but dangerous Reye's syndrome has been observed. It damages the liver and brain.
124186.m: Aspirin is avoided in children with fever because of Reye's syndrome.

124187.q: How is salicylic acid for medicines mostly obtained today?
124187.e: In the past willow bark was used; today salicylic acid is made chemically, cheaply and pure, in large quantities. Acetylsalicylic acid is made from it.
124187.m: Salicylic acid is now made industrially.

124188.q: From which plant is the active substance artemisinin obtained?
124188.e: Artemisinin comes from Artemisia annua, sweet wormwood (annual mugwort). The plant has long been used in traditional Chinese medicine.

124189.q: Which disease are artemisinin and its derivatives mainly used against?
124189.e: Artemisinin derivatives kill the malaria parasites (plasmodia) in the blood very quickly. Today they are part of standard treatment.

124190.q: Which researcher received a Nobel Prize in 2015 for discovering artemisinin?
124190.e: The Chinese pharmacologist Tu Youyou received the 2015 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine. Her group had discovered artemisinin in the 1970s.

124191.q: Which change to the extraction method brought Tu Youyou her decisive success?
a: Extracting at a low temperature instead of boiling
124191.e: An old Chinese text described soaking the wormwood in cold water and squeezing it. Tu Youyou then extracted it with ether at a low temperature and got an effective extract, because heat destroys the active substance.

124192.q: Why does artemisinin work especially well against malaria parasites in red blood cells?
a: It reacts with iron from the blood pigment and forms harmful radicals
It makes the red blood cells bigger
124192.e: The parasites break down haemoglobin in the red blood cells, which releases iron. This splits artemisinin's peroxide bridge, producing radicals that damage the parasite.
124192.m: Artemisinin is activated by iron in the parasite.

124193.q: Why are people also trying to get yeasts to make artemisinin?
a: The amount in the plant is low and varies
124193.e: Sweet wormwood contains only a little artemisinin, and harvests vary. Genetically modified yeasts can make a precursor, which is converted chemically into artemisinin.
124193.m: Yeasts can make a precursor of artemisinin.

124194.q: Why is artemisinin given against malaria in combination with a second active substance?
a: To prevent resistance and kill the remaining parasites
Because on its own it is poisonous
Because otherwise it does not get into the blood
124194.e: Artemisinins work fast but stay in the body only briefly. A longer-acting partner gets rid of the remaining parasites and makes resistance harder, which is why the WHO recommends combination therapies.
124194.m: Against malaria, artemisinin is always given in combination.

124195.q: Which derivative of artemisinin is injected for severe malaria?
124195.e: Artesunate dissolves in water and can therefore be given intravenously. For severe malaria it is now the first-choice medicine.
124195.m: Artesunate is injected for severe malaria.

124196.q: From the bark of which tree was paclitaxel originally isolated?
124196.e: Paclitaxel was found in the bark of Taxus brevifolia in a screening programme run by the US National Cancer Institute. This yew grows in western North America.
124196.m: Paclitaxel originally comes from the Pacific yew.

124197.q: What is paclitaxel used for in medicine?
a: As a cytostatic drug in cancer treatment
124197.e: Paclitaxel stops cell division and so hits fast-growing cancer cells in particular. It is used for breast and lung cancer, among others.

124198.q: How does paclitaxel act on the cell?
a: It stabilises the microtubules and so blocks cell division
It blocks protein production at the ribosomes
124198.e: Normally the microtubules of the spindle are constantly built up and broken down. Paclitaxel prevents them from breaking down, the spindle freezes and mitosis gets stuck.

124199.q: Why was the bark of the Pacific yew not enough as a source of paclitaxel?
a: It contains very little of the substance, and harvesting it kills the trees
It is too hard to grind
The substance breaks down immediately in sunlight
The trees only grow in Antarctica
124199.e: One treatment would have needed the bark of several trees, and yews die when their bark is stripped. That is why other ways of making it were sought.
124199.m: Yew bark was too scarce as a source.

124200.q: From which renewable starting material is paclitaxel made semi-synthetically?
a: From substances in the needles of the European yew
124200.e: The needles contain the precursor 10-deacetylbaccatin III. They can be harvested without killing the tree and converted chemically into paclitaxel.
124200.m: Yew needles provide a precursor for paclitaxel.

124201.q: Why does paclitaxel have a particularly strong effect on cancer cells?
a: Cancer cells have no cell membrane
Cancer cells take up no sugar
124201.e: Paclitaxel blocks cell division. Cells that divide often, such as cancer cells, are therefore hit especially hard.
124201.m: Paclitaxel mainly hits cells that divide often.

124202.q: Which side effect often occurs during chemotherapy with paclitaxel, because healthy cells also divide quickly?
124202.e: Paclitaxel hits all cells that divide quickly, including the cells of the hair roots. The hair usually grows back after the treatment ends.

124203.q: What is the group of active substances called to which paclitaxel and docetaxel belong?
124203.e: The group is named after the genus Taxus, the yew. Docetaxel is a semi-synthetic relative of paclitaxel.

124204.q: On which island did the Netherlands set up large cinchona plantations in the 19th century?
124204.e: Seeds of cinchona trees were taken out of the Andes and planted on Java. This broke the South American monopoly, and the Netherlands soon supplied most of the world's production.
124204.m: Cinchona was later grown mainly on Java.

124205.q: For centuries, quinine was the most important remedy against which disease?
124205.e: Quinine kills malaria parasites in the blood. Synthetic medicines were only added in the 20th century.
124205.m: Quinine was the classic malaria medicine.

124206.q: In which drink does quinine give the bitter taste?
124206.e: Tonic water contains a small amount of quinine as a bitter substance. The amount is much smaller than in a medicinal dose.
124206.m: Tonic water tastes bitter because of quinine.

124207.q: What can you see if you shine UV light on tonic water?
124207.e: Quinine is a fluorescent substance. It absorbs UV light and gives off visible blue light.
124207.m: Quinine glows blue under UV light.

124208.q: Which region do cinchona trees originally come from?
124208.e: Cinchona trees grow wild in the mountain forests of the Andes, for example in Peru and Ecuador. In German they are called “China bark trees”, but the name has nothing to do with China.
124208.m: Cinchona trees come from the Andes.

124209.q: What was cinchona bark called in Europe in the 17th century, because members of a religious order spread it?
124209.e: Jesuits brought the bark from Peru to Europe and made sure it spread. That is why it was also called Jesuits' powder.
124209.m: Cinchona bark used to be called Jesuits' bark.

124210.q: Why may tonic water contain only a little quinine?
a: Because quinine has side effects in larger amounts
Because quinine makes the drink freeze
124210.e: At higher doses quinine is a medicine. Too much of it can cause ringing in the ears, dizziness and problems with vision, which is why the amount in drinks is limited.
124210.m: Quinine is only harmless in small amounts.

124211.q: Which synthetic malaria medicine was developed using quinine as a model?
124211.e: Like quinine, chloroquine is a quinoline derivative. It was very widely used in the 20th century; today many parasites are resistant to it.
124211.m: Chloroquine is a synthetic successor to quinine.

124212.q: Which plant genus does digitoxin come from?
124212.e: Digitoxin is obtained from foxglove species (Digitalis). The name Digitalis comes from the Latin “digitus”, meaning finger.

124213.q: Which group of active substances does digitoxin belong to?
124213.e: Cardiac glycosides consist of a sugar part and a steroid-like aglycone. They act specifically on the heart muscle.

124214.q: How does digitoxin act on the heart muscle?
a: It increases the force with which the heart contracts
It makes the heart beat faster
124214.e: Digitoxin increases the force of contraction (positive inotropic) and slows the heart rate. It used to be a main medicine for heart failure.
124214.m: Digitoxin strengthens the pumping power of the heart.

124215.q: Which transport protein does digitoxin block in heart muscle cells?
124215.e: Blocking the pump raises sodium in the cell, which lets more calcium in. More calcium means a stronger contraction.

124216.q: Why is the common foxglove considered a dangerous poisonous plant?
a: Its substances disturb the heart rhythm
Its roots give off hydrogen cyanide
124216.e: Foxglove contains cardiac glycosides such as digitoxin. Just a few leaves can cause nausea and dangerous heart rhythm problems.
124216.m: Foxglove is very poisonous because of its heart poisons.

124217.q: Why must digitoxin be dosed particularly precisely?
a: The effective dose and the toxic dose are very close together
It is destroyed in the stomach immediately
124217.e: Digitoxin has a narrow therapeutic range. Even a slight overdose can cause dangerous heart rhythm problems.
124217.m: Digitoxin has a narrow therapeutic range.

124218.q: Digitoxin has a half-life of about one week. What does that mean?
a: After about a week, half of it has been broken down
It only works for half a week
After a week it has all been excreted
You have to take it every half week
124218.e: The half-life shows the time after which only half of a substance is left in the body. Digitoxin is broken down slowly by the liver and so stays effective for a long time.
124218.m: Because of its long half-life, digitoxin stays in the body for a long time.

124219.q: Which striking problem with vision is a typical sign of digitalis poisoning?
124219.e: With an overdose, people see colours wrongly, often yellowish. Nausea and heart rhythm problems come on top.
124219.m: Digitalis poisoning can make people see yellow.

124220.q: Why is the foxglove called Digitalis, from the Latin word for finger?
a: Its flowers fit over a fingertip like a sewing thimble
It only grows a finger's breadth tall
Its leaves are divided like fingers
It was described by a doctor called Finger
124220.e: The tube-shaped flowers can be slipped over a fingertip like a thimble. The Latin name Digitalis comes from “digitus”, finger.

a: How people of different cultures use and understand plants
The effect of fertiliser on cereals
124221.e: Ethnobotany combines botany and ethnology. It documents knowledge of plants, for example about medicinal plants, food, fibres or rituals.
124221.m: Ethnobotany studies the relationship between people and plants.

124222.q: Which US biologist is considered the “father of ethnobotany” because of his research in the Amazon region?
124222.e: Richard Evans Schultes lived for years among indigenous peoples of South America. He documented thousands of useful and medicinal plants.
124222.m: Richard Evans Schultes shaped modern ethnobotany.

a: Using traditional knowledge about plants without consent and a fair share of the profits
Cutting down trees in the forest
124223.e: Some companies patented substances based on indigenous knowledge without involving the communities they came from. This is criticised as biopiracy.
124223.m: Biopiracy uses other people's plant knowledge without fair compensation.

124224.q: Which international agreement regulates access to genetic resources and the fair sharing of the benefits?
124224.e: The Nagoya Protocol is part of the Convention on Biological Diversity. Switzerland has ratified it too.
124224.m: The Nagoya Protocol regulates the fair sharing of benefits.

124225.q: Which arrow poison of indigenous peoples of South America led to muscle-relaxing drugs for anaesthesia?
124225.e: Curare paralyses the muscles by blocking the transmission of signals from nerve to muscle. Its active substance tubocurarine was used in anaesthesia.
124225.m: Curare went from arrow poison to an aid in anaesthesia.

124226.q: Which mountain plant does folk medicine, including in the Alpine region, use externally for bruises?
124226.e: Arnica (mountain arnica) contains anti-inflammatory substances. It is only used externally, because it can be poisonous if taken internally.
124226.m: Arnica helps with bruises when used externally.

124227.q: Which well-known substance against malaria comes from the bark of a South American tree?
124227.e: Indigenous peoples of the Andes used the bark of the cinchona tree against fever. Its active substance quinine was long the most important malaria medicine and also gives tonic water its bitter taste.
124227.m: Quinine from cinchona bark works against malaria.

124228.q: From the bark of which tree does the starting substance for aspirin come, which was already used against pain in the past?
124228.e: Willow bark contains salicin, which already helped against fever and pain in folk medicine. Acetylsalicylic acid, known as aspirin, was developed from it.
124228.m: Aspirin goes back to a substance from willow bark.

124229.q: Which anti-cancer substance was obtained from the Madagascar periwinkle, which was known in folk medicine?
124229.e: Researchers studied the Madagascar periwinkle because of its use in folk medicine. They found the vinca alkaloids vinblastine and vincristine, which are used against leukaemias.
124229.m: Vincristine comes from the Madagascar periwinkle.

124230.q: What does the mass balance of a glacier describe?
a: The difference between mass gain and mass loss over a period
The weight of the rock beneath the glacier
The speed of the glacier tongue
124230.e: The mass balance compares accumulation (gain) and ablation (loss), usually over a year. If it is negative, the glacier loses ice.
124230.m: The mass balance shows whether a glacier is growing or shrinking.

124231.q: Why does the measuring year in glacier research in the Alps begin in autumn and not on 1 January?
a: So that winter snow gain and summer melt fall in the same year
Because glaciers flow fastest in autumn
Because most snow falls in autumn
Because no measurements are allowed in January
124231.e: The glaciological budget year usually runs from 1 October to 30 September. This way, accumulation in winter and ablation in summer are in the same year.
124231.m: The glacier year runs from October to September.

124232.q: Which process does NOT belong to the accumulation of a glacier?
a: Snow blown in by the wind
124232.e: Accumulation includes all mass gains, mainly snow. Calving, that is ice breaking off into water, is a mass loss and counts as ablation.
124232.m: Calving is a mass loss of the glacier.

124233.q: Why is a glacier's mass balance converted into water instead of simply giving the thickness of snow and ice?
a: Snow, firn and ice have different densities
Water is easier to measure than ice
124233.e: A metre of fresh snow contains much less water than a metre of ice. That is why the balance is given in metres of water equivalent, so that all forms can be compared.
124233.m: The mass balance is measured in metres of water equivalent.

124234.q: In one year a glacier gains 1.2 m water equivalent from snow and loses 2.0 m through melting. What is its annual balance?
124234.e: Balance equals accumulation minus ablation: 1.2 m minus 2.0 m gives -0.8 m. The negative sign means a loss of mass.
124234.m: The balance is gain minus loss.

124235.q: A glacier with an area of 10 km² has an annual balance of -1 m water equivalent. How much water has it lost?
124235.e: 10 km² is 10,000,000 m². Multiplied by 1 m of water depth this gives 10,000,000 m³, that is 10 million cubic metres.
124235.m: Volume is area times water depth.

124236.q: How does the glaciological method measure melting in the ablation area of a glacier?
a: With stakes drilled into the ice, reading off how much of them is exposed
With weather balloons above the glacier
With thermometers in the rock bed
124236.e: Stakes are drilled into the ice, and later you measure how far they stick out. In the accumulation area, the depth and density of the snow are also measured in snow pits.
124236.m: Stakes show how much ice has melted.

124237.q: What is the geodetic method for determining the mass balance based on?
a: Comparing elevation models of the glacier surface from different years
124237.e: Terrain models are made from aerial photos, laser scans or satellite data. The height difference gives the change in volume, which is converted into mass using an assumed density.
124237.m: The geodetic method compares glacier surfaces.

124238.q: Why does the length of a glacier tongue react only with a delay to a change in mass balance?
a: The ice takes years to decades to flow from the accumulation area to the tongue
The tongue is anchored in the rock
The sun never reaches the tongue
Snow only falls on the tongue
124238.e: A change in mass in the upper part only has an effect once the ice flow has adjusted. That is why large glaciers react more slowly than small ones.
124238.m: Glacier tongues react to the climate with a delay.

124239.q: Through which two main processes does a glacier move down the valley?
a: Internal deformation of the ice and sliding over the bed
Freezing and thawing of the moraines
124239.e: Under its own weight, ice deforms like a very thick mass (creep). When there is meltwater at the bed, the glacier also slides over the ground.

124240.q: Where does a valley glacier flow fastest at its surface?
a: At the left and right edges
124240.e: At the valley sides and the bed, friction slows the ice. In the middle of the surface the distance to these edges is greatest.
124240.m: Glaciers flow fastest in the middle.

124241.q: According to Glen's flow law with n equal to 3, by what factor does the deformation rate increase if the shear stress doubles?
124241.e: The deformation rate is proportional to the stress to the power of 3. 2 to the power of 3 gives 8.
124241.m: Double the stress means eight times the deformation.

124242.q: What are the ice towers called that form in steep icefalls through crossing crevasses?
124242.e: Where the ice flows over a steep step, it tears in many directions. Ice towers are left standing that can collapse at any time.

124243.q: Why are glacier crevasses usually only a few dozen metres deep?
a: Because deeper down the ice flows plastically under pressure and closes crevasses
Because there is always rock beneath
Because crevasses only form in winter
Because water immediately freezes the crevasses shut
124243.e: In the upper metres, ice is brittle and cracks under tension. Deeper down, the pressure from above is so great that the ice flows and squeezes open crevasses shut.
124243.m: Deep crevasses close because of the pressure of the ice.

124244.q: Why can a temperate glacier slide at its bed?
a: The ice at the bed is at the pressure melting point, and meltwater lubricates it
The bed is always covered with grass
The ice there is warmer than 10 °C
The rock under the glacier is magnetic
124244.e: In temperate ice the temperature is at the melting point, which falls slightly under pressure. A film of water at the bed reduces friction, whereas cold glaciers are frozen to their bed.
124244.m: Temperate glaciers slide on a film of water.

124245.q: What is a glacier called that suddenly flows many times faster after a long quiet period?
124245.e: During a surge, the speed rises sharply for months to years, often because of changed water conditions at the bed. It is then followed by another long quiet phase.
124245.m: A surging glacier suddenly advances quickly.

124246.q: Why do especially many crevasses form where a glacier flows over a steep step?
a: The ice is pulled apart there and cracks
The ice there is warmer than 10 °C
The ice freezes especially quickly there
Animals drill holes in the ice there
124246.e: Above a steep step the ice speeds up and is stretched. The brittle ice at the surface cannot withstand this pull and breaks into crevasses and ice towers.
124246.m: Icefalls form where ice is stretched.

124247.q: What does the albedo of a surface state?
a: The share of incoming solar radiation that is reflected
The thickness of the snow cover
The water content of the soil
124247.e: The albedo is the ratio of reflected to incoming shortwave radiation. It lies between 0 (everything absorbed) and 1 (everything reflected).
124247.m: The albedo measures how much a surface reflects.

124248.q: Which surface has the highest albedo?
124248.e: Fresh snow usually reflects about 80 to 90 per cent of sunlight. Dirty ice reflects much less and therefore melts faster.
124248.m: Fresh snow reflects the most light.

124249.q: 800 W/m² of solar radiation falls on a glacier surface, and the albedo is 0.6. How much radiation is absorbed?
124249.e: The share absorbed is 1 minus 0.6, which equals 0.4. 0.4 times 800 W/m² gives 320 W/m².
124249.m: Absorbed is one minus albedo times incoming radiation.

124250.q: Roughly what albedo does bare, clean glacier ice have?
124250.e: Glacier ice contains hardly any air between the crystals and therefore reflects less than snow. Dirty ice is even lower.
124250.m: Glacier ice reflects much less than snow.

124251.q: Why does Saharan dust on Swiss glaciers speed up melting?
a: It darkens the snow and lowers its albedo
It brings warm water with it
124251.e: The reddish dust settles on the snow and lowers how much it reflects. The snow absorbs more solar energy and melts earlier.
124251.m: Saharan dust makes glaciers melt faster.

124252.q: What effect do dark deposits of dust, soot and microorganisms have on a glacier?
a: They absorb more solar energy and encourage melting
They insulate the ice and slow melting
They make the glacier grow faster
They have no effect on the ice
124252.e: Dark deposits, called cryoconite, lower the albedo. They melt their way into the ice and form holes filled with water.
124252.m: Dark glacier dust speeds up melting.
