a: They store more carbon than the atmosphere and plants together
They store less carbon than a single forest
They only release carbon and store none
124963.e: Worldwide, the humus in soils holds more carbon than the atmosphere and all vegetation together. Building up humus can therefore lock away carbon dioxide.
124963.m: Soils are a huge carbon store.

124964.q: Why do we distinguish between nutrient humus and permanent humus?
a: Nutrient humus breaks down quickly, permanent humus lasts a long time
Nutrient humus is mineral, permanent humus is organic
Nutrient humus lies deeper than permanent humus
124964.e: Nutrient humus consists of easily broken-down substances and provides nutrients quickly. Permanent humus made of stable humic substances lasts for decades or centuries and improves soil structure.
124964.m: Permanent humus stays in the soil for a long time.

124965.q: On which parent rock does a rendzina form?
124965.e: A rendzina is a shallow soil on carbonate rock such as limestone, dolomite or gypsum. Its counterpart on silicate rock is called a ranker.

124966.q: Why is a rendzina usually only shallow?
a: Lime dissolves almost completely and leaves little residue
It is blown away by the wind every year
124966.e: During weathering, lime is dissolved by rainwater and carried away. Only a little material is left, from which a thin layer of soil forms over the rock.
124966.m: Rendzinas are thin because lime dissolves almost completely.

124967.q: What lies directly under the dark humus layer in a rendzina?
124967.e: A rendzina has no weathered layer in between. The limestone comes directly below the humus-rich topsoil.
124967.m: In a rendzina, the rock comes directly under the humus.

124968.q: In which Swiss region are rendzinas especially common?
a: In the gneiss area of Ticino
In the Rhône valley on river gravel
124968.e: The Jura is mostly made of limestone. Shallow rendzinas are widespread on its hilltops and slopes.
124968.m: There are many rendzinas in the limestone mountains of the Jura.

124969.q: Which disadvantage is typical of rendzinas as a place for plants to grow?
124969.e: Rendzinas are shallow and stony, so they store only a little water. In summer they dry out quickly.
124969.m: Rendzinas dry out quickly in summer.

124970.q: Which plant community is often found on rendzinas on sunny slopes?
124970.e: On dry, lime-rich rendzinas, species-rich semi-dry grasslands grow, often with orchids. They are among the most species-rich habitats in Switzerland.
124970.m: Species-rich dry grasslands often grow on rendzinas.

124971.q: What pH value does a typical rendzina have?
124971.e: Because the soil lies directly on limestone and contains bits of lime, it is neutral to slightly alkaline. The lime buffers acids.
124971.m: Thanks to lime, rendzinas are neutral to slightly alkaline.

124972.q: Which factor shapes a gley soil?
a: Rainwater that collects and cannot drain
124972.e: Gleys are soils whose lower part lies permanently or at times in groundwater. Soils with trapped rainwater, on the other hand, are called pseudogleys.

124973.q: How can you recognise a gley soil in a soil profile?
a: By grey layers and rust spots
By white salt crusts on the surface
By a red, tropical loam layer
By limestone directly under the grass
124973.e: In the permanently wet subsoil, iron is reduced and colours it grey to blue-green. Where the groundwater rises and falls, iron oxidises into rusty brown spots.
124973.m: Grey colours and rust spots give away a gley.

124974.q: What colour is the permanently wet, oxygen-poor reduction horizon of a gley?
124974.e: When oxygen is lacking, iron is present in its divalent form. These iron compounds colour the soil grey, bluish or greenish.
124974.m: The reduction horizon of a gley is grey-green.

124975.q: What causes the rust spots in the oxidation horizon of a gley?
124975.e: When the groundwater rises and falls, oxygen reaches dissolved iron. It oxidises to trivalent iron and forms rusty brown spots.

124976.q: Unlike a gley, which soil type is shaped by trapped rainwater?
124976.e: In a pseudogley, a dense layer holds back the seepage water. The soil is alternately wet and dry, while a gley is influenced by groundwater.
124976.m: A pseudogley forms from trapped rainwater.

124977.q: Which measure made many gley soils in the Swiss Plateau usable for arable farming?
124977.e: Drainage pipes lowered the groundwater level. This allowed wet gley soils to be ploughed, but wetlands were lost in the process.
124977.m: Drainage made wet soils suitable for crops.

124978.q: Which type of landscape is typical of gley soils?
124978.e: In valley floodplains and hollows, the groundwater is close to the surface. Gleys form there most often.
124978.m: Gleys are found in hollows with high groundwater.

124979.q: In a gley, what does the boundary between the rust-spotted zone and the grey zone show?
a: The depth from which the soil lies permanently in groundwater
Where a glacier used to be
How far the tree roots reach
124979.e: In the rust-spotted zone, the groundwater rises and falls, and air sometimes gets in. Below it, the soil is always wet and poor in oxygen, so it is grey.
124979.m: Below the rust spots, a gley is always wet.

124980.q: What are crop rotation areas (Fruchtfolgeflächen) in Switzerland?
a: All forest areas in the Swiss Plateau
124980.e: Crop rotation areas are the most valuable farmland in Switzerland: well-suited soils that can be ploughed. They are to be kept for arable farming in the long term.
124980.m: Crop rotation areas are Switzerland’s best arable soils.

124981.q: Which federal instrument sets a minimum amount of crop rotation areas for the whole of Switzerland?
a: The Sectoral Plan for Crop Rotation Areas
124981.e: In the Sectoral Plan for Crop Rotation Areas, the federal government decides how much crop rotation land must at least be preserved. The cantons must secure their share permanently.
124981.m: The Sectoral Plan for Crop Rotation Areas protects the best soils.

124982.q: What is the main aim of protecting crop rotation areas?
a: Food security in times of crisis
124982.e: Crop rotation areas are meant to make sure that Switzerland can grow enough food even in a supply crisis. That is why they are specially protected.
124982.m: Crop rotation areas serve security of supply.

124983.q: In which major region of Switzerland are most crop rotation areas?
124983.e: The Swiss Plateau has flat land, deep soils and a mild climate. That is why most of Switzerland’s best arable land is there.
124983.m: Most crop rotation areas are in the Swiss Plateau.

124984.q: Who has to actually designate and secure the crop rotation areas in spatial planning?
124984.e: The federal government sets a quota for each canton. The cantons must show these areas in their structure plans and preserve them.
124984.m: The cantons secure the crop rotation areas.

124985.q: Which danger threatens crop rotation areas in the Swiss Plateau most?
a: Building and sealing of the land
Turning into steppe because of salt
124985.e: The Swiss Plateau is both the best arable land and the most densely populated area. New housing and roads seal valuable soils there.
124985.m: Building is the biggest danger to crop rotation areas.

124986.q: Why do steep slopes usually not count as crop rotation areas?
a: They are hard to farm with machines
No plants grow there at all
They always belong to the federal government
124986.e: Crop rotation areas must be easy to work with machines. That is difficult on steep slopes, and the risk of erosion is greater.
124986.m: Crop rotation areas must be flat enough for machines.

124987.q: What is meant by crop rotation in farming?
a: The planned change of crops on a field
The order of the harvest in autumn
The way the produce travels to market
124987.e: In crop rotation, for example, cereals, root crops and temporary grassland take turns on the same field. This prevents diseases and protects the soil.
124987.m: In crop rotation, crops take turns on a field.

124988.q: What does the term edaphon mean?
a: All the living things in the soil
The pieces of rock in the soil
124988.e: The edaphon includes all organisms living in the soil: bacteria, fungi, algae and soil animals. The term goes back to the biologist Raoul Heinrich Francé.
124988.m: The edaphon is the community of life in the soil.

124989.q: Which organisms are responsible for the typical smell of fresh earth?
124989.e: Actinomycetes are bacteria that produce the scent geosmin. It gives the typical earthy smell, especially after rain.
124989.m: Actinomycetes produce the earthy smell geosmin.

124990.q: Which size group of soil fauna do springtails and mites belong to?
124990.e: Springtails and mites are about 0.2 to 2 millimetres long and count as mesofauna. Single-celled organisms belong to the microfauna, earthworms to the macrofauna.

124991.q: Which soil animal belongs to the megafauna of the soil?
124991.e: The megafauna includes the largest soil dwellers, vertebrates such as moles and voles. Roundworms and ciliates are tiny.
124991.m: The mole belongs to the soil megafauna.

124992.q: What is the device called that drives small animals out of a soil sample using heat and light?
124992.e: In a Berlese funnel, a lamp warms the soil sample from above. The animals flee downwards and fall into a collecting container.
124992.m: A Berlese funnel is used to collect soil animals.

124993.q: What are soil animals such as woodlice and millipedes called, which eat and shred dead plant parts?
124993.e: Woodlice and millipedes shred fallen leaves and so increase their surface area. Then fungi and bacteria can break down the remains faster.

124994.q: Which statement about the number of living things in the soil is true?
a: A handful of soil contains more living things than there are people
A handful of soil contains about a hundred living things
Fewer species live in the soil than on a tree
124994.e: Billions of microorganisms live in a handful of fertile soil. That is more living things than there are people on Earth.
124994.m: A handful of soil contains billions of living things.

124995.q: Which achievement of earthworms especially improves soil structure?
124995.e: Earthworms eat soil and plant remains and mix them in their gut. Their casts contain stable clay-humus complexes that give the soil a crumbly structure.

124996.q: What is meant by soil respiration?
a: The release of carbon dioxide from the soil
The wind in the soil pores
124996.e: In soil respiration, roots, microorganisms and soil animals give off carbon dioxide. It escapes from the soil into the atmosphere.
124996.m: In soil respiration, the soil gives off carbon dioxide.

124997.q: Which two main sources contribute to soil respiration?
124997.e: Autotrophic respiration comes from the plant roots, heterotrophic respiration from microorganisms that break down organic matter.
124997.m: Roots and microorganisms respire in the soil.

124998.q: How does soil air usually differ from the air above the soil?
124998.e: The respiration of soil organisms uses up oxygen and builds up carbon dioxide. Soil air therefore contains many times more carbon dioxide.
124998.m: Soil air contains more carbon dioxide than the air outside.

124999.q: How does soil respiration usually change when soil temperature rises?
a: It increases up to an optimum
124999.e: Warmth speeds up the metabolism of soil organisms. That is why soil respiration rises with temperature, as long as there is enough water.

125000.q: Why is there concern that global warming could be strengthened by soil respiration?
a: Warmer soils break down more humus and release carbon dioxide
125000.e: When temperatures rise, microorganisms break down humus faster. The extra carbon dioxide released can drive warming further.
125000.m: Warmed soils can give off extra carbon dioxide.

125001.q: Which gas can increasingly form instead of carbon dioxide in waterlogged, oxygen-free soils?
125001.e: When there is no oxygen, special microorganisms break down organic substances anaerobically. Among other things, this produces methane, for example in bogs and rice fields.
125001.m: Methane forms in wet soils without oxygen.

125002.q: How big is the global carbon dioxide flow from soil respiration compared with human fossil emissions?
125002.e: Every year, soils release many times the amount of fossil emissions as carbon dioxide. However, a large part is taken up again by photosynthesis.
125002.m: Soil respiration is a huge flow of carbon dioxide.

125003.q: Why is soil respiration often measured in soil biology?
a: As a measure of the activity of microorganisms
To determine the colour of the soil
125003.e: The more carbon dioxide a soil gives off under the same conditions, the more active its microorganisms are. Soil respiration is therefore an important indicator of soil life.
125003.m: Soil respiration shows how active soil life is.

125004.q: Which institution runs Switzerland’s National Soil Monitoring Network (NABO)?
125004.e: NABO is run by Agroscope, the federal centre of excellence for agricultural research. It is commissioned by the Federal Offices for the Environment and for Agriculture.
125004.m: Agroscope runs the National Soil Monitoring Network.

125005.q: Since when has the National Soil Monitoring Network been measuring the state of Swiss soils?
a: Since the founding of the federal state
125005.e: NABO was founded in 1984, when concern about pollutants in soils was growing. Since the first survey in 1985, the same sites have been sampled regularly.
125005.m: NABO has been monitoring soils since the 1980s.

125006.q: Why does the National Soil Monitoring Network (NABO) keep sampling the same sites?
a: To detect long-term changes in the soils
125006.e: Only by studying the same areas over decades can changes such as the build-up of pollutants be reliably shown.
125006.m: NABO tracks changes in soils over a long time.

125007.q: How often are the NABO sites sampled again?
125007.e: The sites are sampled every five years. The samples are also archived so that they can be studied later with new methods.
125007.m: The NABO sites are sampled every five years.

125008.q: According to NABO, which heavy metals have built up on grassland sites with lots of farmyard manure, such as pig slurry?
125008.e: Copper and zinc are added to animal feed and end up on the meadows through the slurry. NABO found an increase in these metals at such sites.
125008.m: Slurry can build up copper and zinc in the soil.

125009.q: Through which fertiliser does the heavy metal cadmium mainly get into arable soils?
125009.e: Rock phosphate naturally contains cadmium. According to NABO, mineral phosphate fertiliser is an important way for cadmium to get into arable soils.
125009.m: Phosphate fertiliser can bring cadmium into the soil.

125010.q: Which ordinance sets the guide values for pollutants in soil in Switzerland?
125010.e: The Ordinance on Soil Pollution (VBBo) sets guide, trigger and clean-up values for pollutants. It is based on the Environmental Protection Act.
125010.m: The VBBo sets pollutant values for soil.

125011.q: Why does NABO keep soil samples in an archive?
a: To study them again later with new methods
125011.e: Archived samples make it possible to measure substances later that were not looked at before. This makes long-term changes easier to prove.
125011.m: Archived soil samples can be studied again later.

125012.q: What is the part of the Earth called where the rock layer, the atmosphere, the water layer and the biosphere overlap and soil forms?
125012.e: The pedosphere is the Earth’s thin layer of soil. Here rock, air, water and living things work together.
125012.m: The pedosphere is the Earth’s soil layer.

125013.q: What is the amount of water called that a well-drained soil can hold against gravity after the seepage water has drained away?
125013.e: Field capacity describes the water held against gravity in the medium and fine pores. Not all of it is available to plants.
125013.m: Field capacity is the water the soil can hold.

125015.q: Why do clay minerals have a very large specific surface area?
a: They consist of tiny, thin flakes
They are hollow inside like tubes
They contain lots of air bubbles
125015.e: Clay minerals are only fractions of a micrometre thick. One gram of clay therefore has a huge surface to which water and nutrients stick.
125015.m: Clay has a huge surface area because of its tiny flakes.

125016.q: Which wood component that is hard to break down is an important starting material for the formation of humic substances?
125016.e: Lignin makes cell walls woody and is broken down only slowly by fungi. A large part of its breakdown products goes into the humic substances.
125016.m: Lignin is an important building block for humic substances.

a: A single layer of carbon atoms in a hexagonal lattice
A carbon crystal made of tetrahedra
A ball made of 60 carbon atoms
A mixture of carbon and silicon
125017.e: Graphene is a layer of carbon only one atom thick, with its atoms arranged in hexagons like a honeycomb. Diamond, on the other hand, is made of tetrahedra.
125017.m: Graphene is a one-atom-thick carbon layer with a honeycomb pattern.

125018.q: What did Andre Geim and Konstantin Novoselov receive the Nobel Prize in Physics for?
125018.e: In 2010 Geim and Novoselov were honoured for their groundbreaking experiments with the two-dimensional material graphene.
125018.m: Geim and Novoselov received the Nobel Prize for graphene.

125019.q: With which surprisingly simple method was graphene first isolated?
125019.e: The researchers used sticky tape to peel off thinner and thinner layers of graphite until single atomic layers were left. This is called mechanical exfoliation.
125019.m: Graphene was first peeled off graphite with sticky tape.

125020.q: What hybridisation do the carbon atoms in graphene have?
125020.e: Each carbon atom is bonded to three neighbours in one plane, which corresponds to sp2 hybridisation. The remaining electron can move across the whole layer.
125020.m: The carbon atoms in graphene are sp2 hybridised.

125021.q: Why is graphene suitable for transparent electrodes, for example in touchscreens?
a: It is almost transparent and conducts electricity well
125021.e: A layer of graphene absorbs only about 2 per cent of light and still conducts electricity very well. This combination is in demand for screens.
125021.m: Graphene is almost transparent and conducts well.

125022.q: Which form of carbon would you get, in theory, if you rolled a graphene layer into a cylinder?
125022.e: Carbon nanotubes are built like rolled-up graphene layers. Fullerenes, on the other hand, are closed cages with pentagons and hexagons.
125022.m: A nanotube is like rolled-up graphene.

125023.q: Why is pure graphene only partly suitable for digital transistors?
a: It does not conduct electricity at all
125023.e: Pure graphene has no band gap and so can hardly be switched off completely. Switching transistors, however, need a clear off state.
125023.m: Without a band gap, graphene is hard to switch off.

125024.q: From the point of view of graphene research, what is graphite made of?
125024.e: In graphite, many graphene layers lie on top of each other and are held together only by weak van der Waals forces. That is why the layers slide easily over each other.
125024.m: Graphite is made of stacked graphene layers.

125025.q: Which element is the most important semiconductor in microelectronics?
125025.e: Silicon is common, can be produced very pure and forms a stable oxide. That is why most computer chips are made of silicon.
125025.m: Silicon is the most important semiconductor.

125026.q: Which element is silicon doped with to produce an n-type semiconductor?
125026.e: Phosphorus has five valence electrons, one more than silicon. This extra electron can move freely and conducts electricity.
125026.m: Phosphorus turns silicon into an n-type semiconductor.

125027.q: How does the electrical conductivity of a pure semiconductor change when the temperature rises?
125027.e: Heat lifts more electrons across the band gap into the conduction band. Unlike metals, a semiconductor therefore conducts better at higher temperatures.

125028.q: What are the missing electrons, which act as positive charges, called in a p-type semiconductor?
125028.e: If an atom is missing a bonding electron, a hole forms. It moves through the crystal like a positive charge as neighbouring electrons move in to fill it.
125028.m: In a p-type semiconductor, holes carry the current.

125029.q: Which component is formed when a p-doped and an n-doped region meet?
125029.e: A depletion layer forms at the pn junction. Current only flows in one direction, and that is the basic function of a diode.
125029.m: A pn junction acts as a diode.

125030.q: Which semiconductor made efficient blue light-emitting diodes possible and earned three researchers a Nobel Prize?
125030.e: Using gallium nitride, Isamu Akasaki, Hiroshi Amano and Shuji Nakamura made efficient blue LEDs. Only then did white LED lamps become possible.
125030.m: Gallium nitride made blue LEDs possible.

125031.q: What are the thin silicon discs on which computer chips are made called?
125031.e: Wafer-thin discs are cut from a large single crystal of silicon. Many chips are made on these wafers at the same time.
125031.m: Computer chips are made on silicon wafers.

125032.q: Which semiconductor is increasingly used in the power electronics of electric cars because it can handle high voltages and temperatures?
125032.e: Silicon carbide has a large band gap and conducts heat well. That is why SiC inverters work more efficiently and can handle higher voltages.
125032.m: Silicon carbide is suited to power electronics.

125033.q: What are perovskites mainly being studied for in energy research at the moment?
a: As the light-absorbing layer in solar cells
As fuel in nuclear power stations
125033.e: Certain perovskites absorb sunlight very well and can be made cheaply. Within a few years, perovskite solar cells reached efficiencies that keep up with silicon.
125033.m: Perovskites are seen as a promising material for solar cells.

125034.q: Which mineral gave the perovskite structure its name?
125034.e: The mineral perovskite is calcium titanate (CaTiO3) and was named after the Russian mineralogist Lev Perovski. All substances with the same crystal structure are also called perovskites.
125034.m: The perovskite structure is named after the mineral calcium titanate.

125035.q: Which toxic heavy metal do most of today’s perovskite solar cells contain?
125035.e: Typical absorbers such as methylammonium lead iodide contain lead. Researchers are therefore looking for safe encapsulation and lead-free alternatives.
125035.m: Many perovskite solar cells contain lead.

125036.q: What is the biggest problem of perovskite solar cells for long-term use?
125036.e: Perovskites break down much faster than silicon when exposed to moisture, heat and light. Long-term stability is therefore the biggest hurdle to bringing them to market.
125036.m: Perovskite cells are not yet stable enough in the long term.

125037.q: Why are perovskite and silicon cells combined in tandem solar cells?
a: They use different parts of the solar spectrum
They then no longer need light
125037.e: The perovskite layer mainly uses high-energy blue light, the silicon cell the red and infrared light. Together they reach efficiencies of over 30 per cent in the laboratory (as of 2025).
125037.m: Tandem cells make better use of sunlight.

125038.q: What does the band gap of the semiconductor in a solar cell determine?
a: Which colours of light the cell can turn into electricity
How large the cell area is
125038.e: Only photons with at least the energy of the band gap can excite electrons and produce electricity. With perovskites, the band gap can be adjusted through their composition.
125038.m: The band gap decides which light a solar cell can use.

125039.q: Which manufacturing advantage makes perovskite solar cells especially interesting?
a: They can be made from solutions at low temperatures
They need diamond as a raw material
They can only be made in space
They are grown from a single giant crystal
125039.e: Perovskite layers can be spin-coated or printed from solution. This uses less energy than producing highly pure silicon.
125039.m: Perovskite layers are easy to make from solution.

125040.q: At which Swiss university did Michael Grätzel develop the dye-sensitised solar cell named after him?
125040.e: Michael Grätzel developed the Grätzel cell at EPFL in Lausanne. His group is also one of the leading ones in perovskite research.
125040.m: Michael Grätzel does research at EPFL in Lausanne.

125041.q: What makes a metallic glass different from an ordinary metal?
a: Its atoms are disordered, that is amorphous
125041.e: Metallic glasses lack the regular crystal structure. The atoms are disordered, as in a liquid that has turned solid.
125041.m: Metallic glasses have no crystal structure.

125042.q: What is the classic way to make a metallic glass?
a: By cooling the melt extremely quickly
By cooling it slowly over weeks
By forging it at room temperature
125042.e: If the melt cools quickly enough, the atoms have no time to arrange themselves into a crystal. This keeps the disordered state.
125042.m: Metallic glass is made by cooling in a flash.

125043.q: Why are metallic glasses often especially resistant to corrosion?
125043.e: Grain boundaries are often weak points where corrosion starts. As metallic glasses have no grains, these weak points are missing.
125043.m: Without grain boundaries, metallic glasses corrode less easily.

125044.q: What are soft magnetic metallic glasses used for in technology?
125044.e: Soft magnetic metallic glasses can be remagnetised with low losses. Transformers with such cores therefore waste less energy.
125044.m: Metallic glasses reduce losses in transformers.

125045.q: Which property limits the size of parts made of metallic glass?
a: The high melting point of over 5000 degrees
125045.e: A part only stays amorphous if it cools quickly enough everywhere. Thick pieces cool too slowly inside and crystallise.
125045.m: Thick parts made of metallic glass cool too slowly.

125046.q: Why can metallic glasses be pressed into moulds when heated, rather like plastic?
a: They become thick and runny before they crystallise
They already melt at room temperature
125046.e: Above the glass transition temperature, metallic glasses become soft and viscous before they crystallise. In this range they can be shaped like thermoplastics.
125046.m: Metallic glasses can be shaped above the glass transition.

125047.q: Which disadvantage limits the use of metallic glass in parts?
a: It can break suddenly when overloaded instead of bending slowly
125047.e: Without a crystal lattice, the deformation is concentrated in thin shear bands. So the material hardly deforms permanently and can fail suddenly.

125048.q: Which mechanical property is typical of metallic glasses?
a: High brittleness like chalk under any load
125048.e: Metallic glasses can deform elastically to a large degree and are very strong. That is why they have been tested in things like springs and sports equipment.
125048.m: Metallic glasses are very strong and elastic.

125049.q: Why does the human body tolerate titanium implants especially well?
a: A thin oxide layer protects the surface
Titanium slowly dissolves in the blood
125049.e: In air, titanium immediately forms a dense layer of titanium dioxide. It is chemically very stable and is considered biocompatible.
125049.m: An oxide layer makes titanium body-friendly.

125050.q: What is the direct growing together of bone with the surface of an implant called?
125050.e: In osseointegration, living bone grows directly onto the implant without connective tissue in between. The Swede Per-Ingvar Brånemark discovered this with titanium.
125050.m: In osseointegration, bone grows together with the implant.

125051.q: What are titanium and titanium alloys used for especially often in medicine?
a: For hip replacements and dental implants
125051.e: Titanium is light, strong and well tolerated. That is why many joint replacements and dental implants are made of titanium or alloys such as Ti-6Al-4V.
125051.m: Titanium is an important material for prostheses and implants.

125052.q: Why is titanium’s lower elastic modulus compared with steel an advantage for implants?
a: The bone is shielded less from load
125052.e: A very stiff implant takes the load off the bone, which can cause the bone to break down. Titanium is about half as stiff as steel and so more like bone.
125052.m: Titanium loads the bone more naturally than steel.

125053.q: Roughly how great is the density of titanium compared with steel?
125053.e: Titanium has a density of about 4.5 grams per cubic centimetre, steel about 7.9. So titanium is much lighter.
125053.m: Titanium is much lighter than steel.

125054.q: Why are people with titanium implants usually allowed into an MRI scanner?
a: Titanium gets cold in the MRI
125054.e: Titanium is hardly attracted by the strong magnetic field because it is not ferromagnetic. However, it can disturb the images near it.
125054.m: Titanium is not attracted by the MRI magnet.

125055.q: Which ceramic material is used as a metal-free alternative to titanium dental implants?
125055.e: Zirconium dioxide implants are tooth-coloured and metal-free. They are used mainly in visible areas of the jaw.
125055.m: Zirconium dioxide is an alternative to titanium implants.

125056.q: Why are implant surfaces often blasted and etched?
a: The roughness helps bone grow onto them
125056.e: A rough, microstructured surface gives bone cells more grip. This speeds up the healing of the implant.
125056.m: Rough surfaces help bone to grow on.

125057.q: Which Swiss engineer invented the hook-and-loop fastener, Velcro, based on burdock burrs?
125057.e: George de Mestral examined burrs that were stuck in his dog’s fur after a walk. Their tiny hooks inspired him to invent Velcro.
125057.m: Velcro was invented by the Swiss George de Mestral.

125058.q: What is the lotus effect of the lotus plant based on?
a: Micro and nano structures with water-repellent wax
Oil given off by the leaves
125058.e: The leaves carry tiny bumps with wax crystals. Water drops rest only on the tips, roll off and take dirt with them.
125058.m: The lotus effect is based on rough, water-repellent structures.

125059.q: Which force lets geckos stick to smooth walls?
125059.e: Geckos’ feet carry millions of very fine hairs. These come so close to the surface that weak van der Waals forces add up to a large sticking force.
125059.m: Geckos stick thanks to van der Waals forces.

125060.q: Which model from nature helped to reduce the drag of swimsuits and aircraft surfaces?
125060.e: The scales of sharks carry fine lengthwise grooves called riblets. They calm the flow at the surface and reduce friction.

125061.q: Which bird was the nose of a Japanese Shinkansen high-speed train modelled on to reduce the tunnel boom?
125061.e: The kingfisher dives into water with almost no splash. The shape of its beak helped reduce the pressure wave when the train enters a tunnel.
125061.m: The kingfisher was the model for a train nose.

125062.q: Which model from nature lies behind light and stiff sandwich panels in aircraft construction?
125062.e: A honeycomb structure made of hexagons is very stiff while using little material. It is used as a core between two thin outer layers.
125062.m: Honeycomb structures make parts light and stiff.

125063.q: What makes spider silk so interesting for materials research?
a: It is very tear-resistant and stretchy at the same time
It conducts electricity better than copper
It is fireproof up to 3000 degrees
125063.e: Spider silk combines high tensile strength with great stretchiness. Relative to its weight, it can absorb more energy than many steels.
125063.m: Spider silk is both tear-resistant and stretchy.

a: Using solutions from nature in technology
125064.e: The word combines biology and technology. Engineers transfer principles from nature to technical products instead of copying living things directly.
125064.m: Bionics transfers ideas from nature into technology.

125065.q: How does electrochromic glass change its tint?
a: By heating it with a hairdryer
125065.e: In electrochromic glass, ions move into a thin layer when a voltage is applied and change how much light it lets through. This means windows can be darkened at the push of a button.
125065.m: Electrochromic glass darkens when a voltage is applied.

125066.q: What happens to a bent wire made of a shape memory alloy when you heat it?
a: It returns to its original shape
125066.e: When heated, the crystal lattice changes and the material returns to its stored shape. Experts call this the martensite to austenite transformation.
125066.m: Shape memory alloys return to their shape when heated.

125067.q: What happens to a piezoelectric material when you squeeze it?
125067.e: Pressure shifts the centres of charge in the crystal so that a voltage appears at the surface. The other way round, the material changes shape when a voltage is applied.
125067.m: Piezoelectric materials produce a voltage under pressure.

a: The brothers Jacques and Pierre Curie
125068.e: The Curie brothers demonstrated the effect in the 19th century in crystals such as quartz. Today it is used in lighters, sensors and quartz watches.

125069.q: How does a magnetorheological fluid react to a magnetic field?
125069.e: The fluid contains fine iron particles that line up in chains in a magnetic field. This greatly increases the viscosity, which is used in adaptive shock absorbers.
125069.m: Magnetorheological fluids become thick in a magnetic field.

125070.q: Which smart material darkens by itself in sunlight, for example in spectacle lenses?
125070.e: Photochromic lenses contain substances that change under UV light and make the glass darker. In the shade they become light again.

125071.q: What does Empa use an iron-based shape memory alloy for in construction?
a: To prestress and strengthen concrete structures afterwards
125071.e: The bars are built in and then heated. Because they try to contract, they prestress the structure and strengthen things like existing bridges.
125071.m: Shape memory steel can prestress concrete structures.

125072.q: What is meant by the superelasticity of a shape memory alloy?
a: Large deformation that reverses by itself when the load is removed
125072.e: Above a certain temperature, a shape memory alloy can be deformed a lot and springs back when the load is removed. The reason is a phase change caused by the stress.
125072.m: Superelastic alloys spring back after large deformation.

125073.q: Which disadvantage is typical of high-performance ceramics?
125073.e: Ceramics are hard, heat-resistant and hard-wearing, but can hardly give way plastically. So a crack spreads easily.
125073.m: High-performance ceramics are hard but brittle.

125074.q: What is the manufacturing step called in which ceramic powder is compacted into a solid body below its melting point?
125074.e: During sintering, the powder grains grow together at high temperature without fully melting. Pores close up and the part becomes dense.

125075.q: Which oxide ceramic is often used for the ball heads of hip replacements?
125075.e: Aluminium oxide is very hard, smooth and well tolerated by the body. Ball heads made from it wear very little.
125075.m: Aluminium oxide is used for hip balls.

125076.q: What is zirconium dioxide used for in dentistry?
125076.e: Zirconium dioxide is very strong, tooth-coloured and well tolerated. It is one of the toughest ceramics and often replaces metal in dental work.
125076.m: Dental crowns are often made of zirconium dioxide.

125077.q: Where are high-performance ceramics used because of their heat resistance?
a: In the heat shield of space shuttles
125077.e: Ceramic tiles, for example, protected the Space Shuttle from temperatures of over 1000 degrees when it entered the atmosphere.
125077.m: Ceramics protect spacecraft from great heat.

125078.q: For which use is silicon nitride valued because of its hardness and low density?
125078.e: Silicon nitride balls are lighter and harder than steel balls. They are suitable for bearings that spin very fast.
125078.m: Silicon nitride is suitable for bearing balls.

125079.q: Why do ceramic parts often break suddenly without bending first?
a: Small cracks or pores spread all at once
Ceramics become liquid in the cold
125079.e: Ceramics can hardly deform plastically. A tiny flaw such as a pore becomes the starting point of a crack that spreads very quickly.
125079.m: Ceramics break at their biggest flaw.

125080.q: Which fibre-reinforced ceramic material is used for high-performance brake discs?
125080.e: Carbon fibres in a silicon carbide matrix make the ceramic less likely to break. Such brake discs are light and can handle high temperatures.
125080.m: Ceramic brakes are made of fibre-reinforced silicon carbide.

125081.q: Why does wood swell and shrink when the humidity changes?
a: Its cell walls take in and give off water
It contains air bubbles that expand
Its growth rings keep growing after felling
125081.e: The cell walls of wood bind water between the cellulose fibres. When the moisture in the wood rises, it swells; when it falls, it shrinks.
125081.m: Wood swells and shrinks with moisture.

125082.q: Where does the name graphene come from?
a: From graphite, of which it is a single layer
From the Greek word for water
125082.e: Graphene is a single atomic layer of graphite. The ending “-ene” is also known from other carbon compounds.

125083.q: Which sea creature is the model for adhesives that also stick underwater?
125083.e: Blue mussels attach themselves to wet rocks with sticky threads. Their adhesive proteins inspire glues for medicine and technology.
125083.m: Mussels are the model for underwater glue.

125084.q: What is the name of Empa’s modular research building in Dübendorf, where new building and wood technologies are tested in everyday use?
125084.e: In NEST, new building methods, materials and energy systems are tried out in units that are lived in and used. The modules can be swapped.
125084.m: Empa tests new building technologies in NEST.

125085.q: What did Empa researchers treat spruce and maple wood with to improve the sound of violins?
125085.e: Selected fungi break down the cell walls slightly in a controlled way. The wood becomes lighter, and the violins sound similar to old master instruments.
125085.m: Fungi can improve tonewood for violins.

125086.q: What property did researchers at Empa and ETH give wood by partly removing the lignin and so making it squeezable?
a: It produces an electrical voltage when pressed
125086.e: The sponge-like wood deforms a lot under pressure. The piezoelectric effect of the cellulose then produces a measurable voltage.
125086.m: Treated wood can produce electricity under pressure.

125087.q: Which three main components make up the cell walls of wood?
125087.e: Cellulose forms fibres that resist pulling, hemicellulose links them, and lignin makes the cell wall resist pressure. Together they form a natural composite material.
125087.m: Wood is made of cellulose, hemicellulose and lignin.

125088.q: Why is wood considered an anisotropic material?
a: Its properties depend on the direction of the grain
It is equally strong in all directions
It is made of only one element
It conducts electricity equally in every direction
125088.e: Along the grain, wood is much stronger and stiffer than across it. Shrinking and swelling also differ depending on the direction.
125088.m: Wood behaves differently depending on the grain direction.

125089.q: Why is using wood in construction considered climate-friendly?
a: It stores carbon that the tree absorbed
It gives off oxygen once built in
125089.e: As trees grow, they take carbon dioxide out of the air. As long as the wood is part of a building, this carbon stays stored.
125089.m: Wood used in buildings stores carbon.

125090.q: Roughly what compressive strength does ultra-high-performance concrete reach?
125090.e: Normal concrete reaches about 20 to 50 megapascals. Ultra-high-performance concrete reaches over 150 megapascals, several times as much.
125090.m: Ultra-high-performance concrete is several times stronger than normal concrete.

125091.q: Which fine additive fills the gaps between the cement grains in ultra-high-performance concrete?
125091.e: Silica fume is made of tiny spheres that are much smaller than cement grains. It fills the gaps and also reacts chemically with the hardened cement paste.
125091.m: Silica fume makes concrete especially dense.

125092.q: How does ultra-high-performance concrete differ from normal concrete in its water-cement ratio?
a: It has a very low water-cement ratio
It has a very high water-cement ratio
It contains no cement at all
It contains no water at all
125092.e: With little water, hardly any capillary pores are left after hardening. So that the concrete can still be worked, superplasticisers are added.
125092.m: Little water makes concrete dense and strong.

125093.q: Why are fine steel fibres often mixed into ultra-high-performance concrete?
125093.e: Without fibres, the very strong concrete would be brittle. The steel fibres bridge cracks and make it tough and strong in tension.
125093.m: Steel fibres make ultra-high-performance concrete tough.

125094.q: What is ultra-high-performance concrete often used for in Switzerland?
a: To strengthen and seal bridge decks
125094.e: A thin layer of ultra-high-performance concrete protects bridge decks from water and road salt and strengthens them at the same time. This lets existing bridges be used for longer.
125094.m: Ultra-high-performance concrete protects and strengthens bridges.

125095.q: Why is ultra-high-performance concrete especially durable against road salt?
a: Its dense structure lets hardly any chlorides in
It contains a lot of salt itself
125095.e: Because of the extremely low porosity, water and chlorides can hardly get in. This protects the reinforcement and fibres from corrosion.
125095.m: Dense concrete protects against road salt.

125096.q: What substance is silica fume mainly made of?
125096.e: Silica fume consists of tiny spheres of amorphous silicon dioxide. In concrete it reacts with the cement paste and makes it denser and stronger.
125096.m: Silica fume is mainly silicon dioxide.

125097.q: Which principle lies behind the recipe for ultra-high-performance concrete?
a: The highest possible packing density of the grains
The largest possible stones in the mix
As many air pores as possible
125097.e: Fine and coarser ingredients are matched so that they fill each other’s gaps. The denser the packing, the stronger the concrete.
125097.m: High packing density makes concrete strong.

125098.q: Which equation describes the condition for X-ray reflections from crystal lattice planes?
125098.e: The Bragg equation says n times the wavelength equals 2 d times the sine of the angle. It links wavelength, lattice plane spacing and diffraction angle.
125098.m: The Bragg equation describes X-ray diffraction by a crystal.

125099.q: For X-ray diffraction, n · λ = 2 · d · sin θ. X-rays with λ = 0.154 nm give a first-order reflection (n = 1) at θ = 30°. What is the lattice plane spacing d?
125099.e: Rearranged, d = λ ÷ (2 · sin 30°). With sin 30° = 0.5, this gives d = 0.154 nm ÷ 1 = 0.154 nm.
125099.m: At 30 degrees the lattice plane spacing equals the wavelength.

125100.q: Who discovered that X-rays are diffracted by crystals?
125100.e: Max von Laue showed that crystals act as diffraction gratings for X-rays. This proved the wave nature of the radiation and the lattice structure of crystals.
125100.m: Max von Laue discovered X-ray diffraction by crystals.

125101.q: How are X-rays produced in an X-ray tube?
a: Fast electrons hit a metal anode
Light passes through a glass prism
125101.e: In the tube, electrons are accelerated by a high voltage. When they hit the anode, often made of copper or tungsten, they give off energy as X-rays.
125101.m: X-rays are produced when fast electrons hit metal.

125102.q: Which physicist is the largest federal research institute for natural and engineering sciences in Villigen named after?
125102.e: The Paul Scherrer Institute is named after the physicist who, with Peter Debye, developed the Debye-Scherrer method of powder diffraction. The Swiss Light Source synchrotron is also there.
125102.m: The PSI bears the name of Paul Scherrer.

125103.q: Why do amorphous substances show no sharp reflections in an X-ray diffraction pattern?
a: They lack a regular long-range order
They consist of only one element
125103.e: Sharp reflections only come from regularly repeated lattice planes. Amorphous substances therefore produce only broad, blurred humps.
125103.m: Amorphous substances give no sharp X-ray reflections.

125104.q: What condition must a part meet for eddy current testing?
a: It must be made of ceramic
125104.e: A coil produces eddy currents in the part, which are disturbed by cracks. This only works in electrically conductive materials such as metals.
125104.m: Eddy current testing needs conductive materials.

125105.q: What is X-ray powder diffraction mainly used for in materials analysis?
a: To measure the elongation at break
125105.e: Every crystalline phase produces a characteristic diffraction pattern, like a fingerprint. By comparing it with databases, the phases can be identified.
125105.m: X-ray diffraction shows which crystal phases are present.

125106.q: Whose X-ray diffraction image “Photo 51” helped to reveal the double helix structure of DNA?
125106.e: Rosalind Franklin and her PhD student Raymond Gosling took the famous diffraction image. It showed the typical cross pattern of a helix.
125106.m: Rosalind Franklin’s “Photo 51” showed the DNA helix.

125107.q: A steel bar with a cross-section of 100 square millimetres is pulled with 10 kilonewtons. What is the stress?
125107.e: Stress is force divided by area: 10,000 N divided by 100 mm² gives 100 N/mm², which is 100 MPa.

125108.q: Steel has a Young’s modulus of 210 gigapascals. What stress is there in the elastic range at a strain of 0.1 per cent?
125108.e: According to Hooke’s law, stress is Young’s modulus times strain: 210,000 MPa times 0.001 gives 210 MPa.
125108.m: In the elastic range, stress is proportional to strain.

125109.q: Which material property is tested with the Charpy impact test?
125109.e: A pendulum hammer smashes a notched sample, and the energy used is measured. This shows whether a steel becomes brittle at low temperatures.

125110.q: Which diagram shows how many load cycles a part can withstand at a certain stress amplitude before a fatigue fracture?
125110.e: In the 19th century, August Wöhler studied broken railway axles. The diagram named after him shows the service life under changing loads.
125110.m: The Wöhler diagram describes material fatigue.

125111.q: Which method is part of non-destructive materials testing?
125111.e: In ultrasonic testing, sound waves are sent into the part and reflected by internal flaws. The part is not damaged.
125111.m: Ultrasound finds flaws without destroying the part.

125112.q: What is the slow, time-dependent deformation of a material under a constant load at high temperature called?
125112.e: Under constant load and heat, materials gradually keep deforming, even below the yield point. Creep is important, for example, for turbine blades.
125112.m: Under heat and constant load, materials creep.

125113.q: What is the science called that studies biological rhythms such as the body clock?
125113.e: The word comes from the Greek “chronos” (time). Chronobiology studies things such as the sleep-wake rhythm, jet lag and shift work.

125114.q: Roughly how long does one cycle of the body clock in the body's cells last?
125114.e: The body clock is based on genes that switch themselves on and off in a feedback loop. One cycle lasts about a day, hence the name circadian rhythm.
125114.m: The body clock ticks in a rhythm of about 24 hours.

125115.q: What do single nerve cells of the suprachiasmatic nucleus show when they are kept in a cell culture?
a: They keep their own daily rhythm.
125115.e: Even when isolated, the activity and gene reading of these cells vary with a period of about 24 hours. So the clock is in every single cell.
125115.m: Single cells of the master clock keep ticking even on their own.

125116.q: Which feeling becomes stronger as adenosine builds up in the brain during the day?
125116.e: The longer you are awake, the more adenosine builds up in the brain. It dampens the nerve cells and creates sleep pressure.

125117.q: What is the time from falling asleep to the start of the first REM phase called?
125117.e: REM latency is fairly long in healthy people, because the non-REM stages come first. A very short REM latency can point to an illness.
125117.m: REM latency measures the time until the first REM phase.

125118.q: Someone spends 8 hours in bed and sleeps for 6 of them. What is their sleep efficiency?
125118.e: Sleep efficiency is the time asleep divided by the time in bed. 6 divided by 8 gives 0.75, which is 75 per cent.
125118.m: Sleep efficiency compares the time asleep with the time in bed.

125119.q: What is measured with an EEG in a sleep laboratory?
125119.e: The electroencephalogram uses electrodes on the scalp to measure the electrical activity of the brain. This shows the stages of sleep.
125119.m: The EEG shows the brain waves during sleep.

125120.q: In which sleep phase is it hardest to wake someone up?
a: In light sleep shortly before waking
125120.e: In deep sleep, the brain is greatly slowed down. People woken from it are often especially groggy.
125120.m: Deep sleep is the hardest to wake up from.

125121.q: What is the temporary grogginess and reduced performance straight after waking up called?
125121.e: Sleep inertia can last from a few minutes to over half an hour. It is particularly strong when you are woken from deep sleep.
125121.m: Right after waking up, sleep inertia dampens performance.

125122.q: Roughly how long does a sleep cycle of non-REM and REM sleep last?
125122.e: One cycle lasts about 90 minutes. During a night you therefore go through four to six of these cycles.
125122.m: A sleep cycle lasts about one and a half hours.

125123.q: How does the proportion of REM sleep change during the night?
a: It stays the same all night
It only occurs in the first hour
125123.e: In the first half of the night, deep sleep dominates. Towards morning the REM phases get longer, which is why you often remember dreams from shortly before waking.
125123.m: REM sleep gets longer towards morning.

125124.q: Why do you hardly move in REM sleep despite vivid dreams?
a: The skeletal muscles are largely paralysed
The brain is completely switched off then
The heart does not beat then
You are unconscious as under anaesthetic
125124.e: In REM sleep, the muscles are strongly inhibited and only the eyes and breathing muscles move. This stops you acting out your dreams with real movements.
125124.m: In REM sleep the muscles are almost paralysed.

125125.q: In sleep medicine, what is meant by an arousal?
a: A brief waking reaction on the EEG lasting at least 3 seconds
Waking up completely in the morning
125125.e: An arousal is a sudden switch to faster brain waves for a few seconds. People often do not notice these brief waking reactions.
125125.m: An arousal is a brief, often unnoticed waking reaction.

125126.q: How is airflow measured in a sleep laboratory?
a: With sensors at the nose and mouth
With a clip on the earlobe
With a thermometer in the ear
125126.e: Small sensors in front of the nose and mouth record the airflow or changes in temperature during breathing. This reveals pauses in breathing and shallow breathing.
125126.m: Airflow is measured at the nose and mouth.

125127.q: Why are leg movements also recorded in a sleep laboratory?
a: To identify restless legs as a cause of poor sleep
125127.e: Some people move their legs again and again in their sleep and briefly wake up as a result. Electrodes on the legs make these movements visible.

125128.q: What is it called when many people sleep worse during their first night in a sleep laboratory?
125128.e: The unfamiliar surroundings and the cables disturb sleep on the first night. That is why measurements are sometimes taken over two nights.
125128.m: People often sleep worse on their first night in a sleep laboratory.

a: A marked flattening of breathing with a drop in oxygen or a waking reaction
A complete stop in breathing lasting over a minute
125129.e: In a hypopnoea, the airflow is greatly reduced but not completely interrupted. Like apnoea, it counts as a breathing disorder during sleep.
125129.m: A hypopnoea is a strong flattening of breathing.

125130.q: Which treatment is most commonly used for obstructive sleep apnoea?
a: A breathing mask with slight positive pressure (CPAP)
125130.e: The CPAP machine blows air with slight positive pressure into the airways through a mask. This keeps the throat open during sleep.
125130.m: A CPAP mask keeps the airways open during sleep.

125131.q: What is the main feature of narcolepsy?
a: Severe daytime sleepiness with sudden falling asleep
Loud snoring with pauses in breathing
125131.e: People with narcolepsy can hardly stay awake during the day and sometimes fall asleep in the middle of an activity. The cause is a disorder in the brain's control of sleeping and waking.
125131.m: Narcolepsy causes severe sleepiness during the day.

125132.q: On which day of the week is the conflict between the body clock and the alarm time usually greatest with social jet lag?
125132.e: After sleeping late at the weekend, the body clock has shifted later. On Monday morning the alarm then rings especially early in your internal night.
125132.m: Monday morning is especially hard with social jet lag.

125133.q: What is the aim of sleep restriction in the treatment of insomnia?
a: To match the time in bed to the actual sleep time in order to increase sleep pressure
To spend as many hours as possible in bed
To sleep only during the day
To stay awake all night every night
125133.e: People who lie awake in bed for a long time sleep in fragments. Shortening the time in bed increases sleep pressure, and sleep becomes deeper and more continuous.
125133.m: Sleep restriction shortens the time in bed so that sleep becomes deeper.

125134.q: What is recommended about eating in the evening for a good night's sleep?
a: No heavy meals shortly before going to bed
A big meal right before going to sleep
Eating nothing at all after midday
Only very spicy food in the evening
125134.e: A heavy meal keeps the digestion busy and can make it harder to fall asleep. A light meal a few hours before sleeping is better.
125134.m: A heavy evening meal shortly before sleeping disturbs your night's rest.

125135.q: What does the word “circadian” literally mean?
125135.e: The word comes from the Latin “circa” (about) and “dies” (day). It refers to biological rhythms with a period of about 24 hours.
125135.m: Circadian rhythms last about a day.

125136.q: On average, how long is the internal period of the human clock when all external time cues are missing?
125136.e: Without time cues, the body clock of most people runs a little longer than 24 hours. That is why it has to be adjusted to the day anew every day.
125136.m: The human body clock usually runs a little slower than the 24-hour day.

125137.q: In which model organism were the molecular mechanisms of the body clock researched that were awarded the Nobel Prize in Medicine in 2017?
125137.e: Jeffrey Hall, Michael Rosbash and Michael Young studied clock genes in the fruit fly Drosophila. For this they received the 2017 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine.
125137.m: The molecular body clock was first decoded in the fruit fly.

125138.q: Which hormone does the body typically release in particularly large amounts shortly after waking in the morning?
125138.e: The cortisol level rises in the second half of the night and peaks shortly after waking. Cortisol helps to provide energy for the day.
125138.m: Cortisol reaches its peak in the morning after waking.

125139.q: When does the core body temperature of a person with a normal sleep rhythm typically reach its minimum?
a: In the early hours of the morning
125139.e: Core temperature follows a circadian rhythm and is lowest in the second half of the night, a few hours before waking. It is highest in the late afternoon.
125139.m: Body temperature is lowest in the early hours of the morning.

125140.q: What do you call a biological rhythm that continues with its own period without external time cues?
125140.e: In isolation experiments without daylight and clocks, the rhythm runs freely with its own period. It then shifts a little each day compared with clock time.
125140.m: A free-running rhythm follows only its own period.

125141.q: Why is adjusting to the time difference after an eastward flight usually harder than after a westward one?
a: The body clock has to be put forward, which is harder.
There is less sunlight during the day in the east.
The air pressure in the plane is lower when flying east.
Eastward flights always take much longer.
125141.e: Because the internal period is usually a little longer than 24 hours, it is easier to shift the clock later. After an eastward flight, however, you have to sleep earlier, which means putting the clock forward.
125141.m: Flying east requires putting the body clock forward and is therefore harder.

125142.q: What are biological rhythms called whose period is much shorter than a day, such as the sleep cycle at night?
125142.e: Ultradian rhythms repeat several times a day. Infradian rhythms, on the other hand, last longer than a day, and circannual ones about a year.
125142.m: Ultradian rhythms run several times a day.

125143.q: What does the name “suprachiasmatic” refer to?
a: Its position above the crossing of the optic nerves
Its connection to the spinal cord
125143.e: “Supra” means above, and the “optic chiasm” is where the optic nerves cross. The nucleus lies directly above it and so easily receives signals from the eyes.
125143.m: The suprachiasmatic nucleus lies above the crossing of the optic nerves.

125144.q: Where does the master clock in the brain get the information about whether it is day or night?
a: From the retina of the eyes
From the skin via the temperature
125144.e: A special nerve pathway leads directly from the retina to the suprachiasmatic nucleus. It reports brightness, not images.
125144.m: Light reaches the master clock through the eyes.

125145.q: Which light shifts the body clock particularly strongly in the evening, for example from a mobile phone screen?
125145.e: Special cells in the retina react mainly to blue light and report it to the body clock. In the evening it inhibits the production of melatonin and delays falling asleep.
125145.m: Blue light in the evening shifts the body clock.

125146.q: What happens in laboratory animals when the suprachiasmatic nucleus is destroyed?
a: The sleep-wake rhythm loses its daily order.
The animals no longer sleep at all.
Their body temperature rises sharply for good.
125146.e: Without the master clock, sleep and activity are spread randomly over day and night. The animals still sleep, but no longer in a daily rhythm.
125146.m: Without the suprachiasmatic nucleus, there is no orderly daily rhythm.

125147.q: What did transplant experiments show in which hamsters without their own master clock received the suprachiasmatic nucleus of another animal?
a: The animals took on the rhythm of the donor animal.
The animals had no rhythm at all.
The animals always rejected the tissue.
125147.e: After the transplant, the recipients showed the donor's period, not their own previous period. This proved that the nucleus itself sets the pace.
125147.m: A transplanted suprachiasmatic nucleus brings its own rhythm with it.

125148.q: What are the clocks in organs such as the liver or heart called that are coordinated by the suprachiasmatic nucleus?
125148.e: Almost every cell in the body has its own molecular clock. The master clock in the brain coordinates these peripheral clocks with each other.
125148.m: Peripheral clocks in the organs are coordinated by the master clock in the brain.

125149.q: The breakdown of which molecule is the main source of adenosine in cells?
125149.e: ATP (adenosine triphosphate) is the energy carrier of the cells. When it is used up, adenosine is produced in several steps.
125149.m: Adenosine is a breakdown product of the energy carrier ATP.

125150.q: How does caffeine make you more alert?
a: It breaks down adenosine in the blood.
It activates the suprachiasmatic nucleus directly.
125150.e: Caffeine resembles adenosine and occupies its receptors without activating them. As a result, the tiredness signal gets through less well.
125150.m: Caffeine blocks the docking sites for adenosine.

125151.q: Why can a coffee in the evening make it harder to fall asleep?
a: Caffeine blocks the tiredness signal of adenosine
125151.e: Caffeine occupies the adenosine receptors in the brain. Because it works for hours, the tiredness signal gets through less well in the evening.
125151.m: Caffeine in the evening can disturb sleep.

125152.q: According to the two-process model, which two processes control when we sleep?
a: Sleep pressure and the body clock
125152.e: Sleep pressure rises the longer we are awake, and the body clock follows a daily rhythm. The model was developed by the Zurich researcher Alexander Borbély.
125152.m: Sleep pressure and the body clock together determine sleep.

125153.q: What does “Process S” stand for in the two-process model of sleep regulation?
125153.e: Process S rises the longer you are awake and falls during sleep. Process C, by contrast, is the circadian rhythm of the body clock.
125153.m: Process S describes the sleep pressure that rises the longer you are awake.

125154.q: Which measuring method is used to record brain waves during sleep?
125154.e: In an EEG, electrodes on the scalp measure the electrical activity of the brain. This shows sleep phases such as deep sleep and REM sleep.
125154.m: The EEG shows the brain waves.

125155.q: Roughly what is the half-life of caffeine in healthy adults?
125155.e: After about 5 hours, half of the caffeine has been broken down, although the values vary greatly from person to person. A coffee in the late afternoon can therefore still affect sleep.
125155.m: Caffeine keeps working for many hours after you drink it.

125156.q: Which two building blocks make up the nucleoside adenosine?
125156.e: Adenosine consists of the base adenine bound to the sugar ribose. When phosphate groups are added, nucleotides are formed.
125156.m: Adenosine is made of adenine and ribose.

125157.q: How many non-REM stages does the classification now used by the American Academy of Sleep Medicine distinguish?
125157.e: The AASM distinguishes the stages N1, N2 and N3 as well as REM sleep. N3 corresponds to deep sleep.
125157.m: Today non-REM sleep is divided into three stages.

125158.q: What does pulse oximetry measure during a sleep study?
a: The oxygen saturation of the blood
The carbon dioxide content of the room air
The brain waves in deep sleep
125158.e: A sensor on the finger uses light to measure what percentage of the haemoglobin is carrying oxygen. Drops in saturation point to pauses in breathing.
125158.m: Pulse oximetry measures the oxygen saturation in the blood.

125159.q: Which sleep phase can be recognised in polysomnography by rapid eye movements and relaxed muscles?
125159.e: REM stands for “Rapid Eye Movement”. In this phase you dream especially vividly, while the body's muscles are almost paralysed.
125159.m: In REM sleep the eyes move quickly.

125160.q: Which sleep disorder can be easily recognised with video polysomnography because those affected act out their dreams physically?
125160.e: In REM sleep behaviour disorder, the normal muscle paralysis during REM sleep is missing. Those affected hit or kick in their dreams, which is visible on video and in the EMG.
125160.m: In REM sleep behaviour disorder, dreams are acted out.

125161.q: What is typically missing in home polygraphy compared with polysomnography in a sleep laboratory?
125161.e: Polygraphy mainly records breathing and oxygen, but usually no EEG. That is why it cannot determine the stages of sleep.
125161.m: Home polygraphy usually does not measure brain waves.

125162.q: From what duration does a pause in breathing during sleep count as an apnoea?
125162.e: An apnoea is a pause in breathing of 10 seconds or more. Shorter pauses do not count as an apnoea.
125162.m: An apnoea lasts at least ten seconds.

125163.q: What does the apnoea-hypopnoea index (AHI) indicate?
a: The number of breathing pauses and shallow breaths per hour of sleep
The length of the longest pause in breathing
The lowest oxygen value of the night
The number of snoring noises per night
125163.e: The AHI counts apnoeas and hypopnoeas and divides them by the hours of sleep. It is used to classify how severe the condition is.
125163.m: The AHI counts the breathing disturbances per hour of sleep.

125164.q: Which risk factor particularly encourages obstructive sleep apnoea?
125164.e: Fatty tissue around the neck narrows the upper airways. During sleep the muscles relax and the throat collapses more easily.
125164.m: Being overweight increases the risk of sleep apnoea.

125165.q: How does obstructive sleep apnoea differ from central sleep apnoea?
a: In the obstructive type the upper airways collapse even though there is breathing effort.
In the obstructive type there is no drive to breathe from the brain at all.
The obstructive type only occurs while awake.
The obstructive type only affects the lungs themselves.
125165.e: In the obstructive type, the body tries to breathe but the throat is blocked. In the central type, the breathing centre briefly sends no signals.
125165.m: In obstructive sleep apnoea, no air moves despite breathing effort.

125166.q: Which main daytime symptom often occurs with untreated sleep apnoea?
a: An increased urge to move the legs
125166.e: Because of the many brief waking reactions, sleep is not restful. Those affected easily nod off during the day, which is dangerous when driving, for example.
125166.m: Sleep apnoea often makes people very sleepy during the day.

125167.q: Which cardiovascular disease is encouraged by untreated obstructive sleep apnoea?
125167.e: With every pause in breathing, the body reacts with a stress response and a rise in blood pressure. Over the years this increases the risk of permanent high blood pressure.
125167.m: Untreated sleep apnoea increases the risk of high blood pressure.

125168.q: Which alternative to mask therapy is often used for mild to moderate obstructive sleep apnoea?
125168.e: The splint pushes the lower jaw slightly forwards during sleep. This keeps the throat more open.
125168.m: A lower jaw splint can keep the airways open during sleep.

125169.q: In narcolepsy, what is meant by cataplexy?
a: A sudden loss of muscle tone triggered by emotions
125169.e: In cataplexy, the muscles suddenly go limp, for example when laughing or being surprised. The person stays conscious throughout.
125169.m: Cataplexy is a loss of muscle tone triggered by emotions.

125170.q: What is the job of the messenger substance that is missing in type 1 narcolepsy?
a: It keeps us steadily awake during the day
125170.e: In type 1 narcolepsy, nerve cells in the hypothalamus that produce orexin are lost. Without this messenger substance, the brain easily tips from waking into sleep.
125170.m: In type 1 narcolepsy, a messenger substance that keeps us awake is missing.

125171.q: Which test in a sleep laboratory measures how quickly someone falls asleep on several occasions during the day?
125171.e: In the multiple sleep latency test, the person is allowed to lie down several times spread over the day. Short times to fall asleep and early REM phases point to narcolepsy.
125171.m: The multiple sleep latency test measures the tendency to fall asleep during the day.

125172.q: What is typical of narcolepsy on a sleep EEG?
a: REM sleep starts soon after falling asleep.
The eyes do not move at all during sleep.
125172.e: Normally the first REM sleep only comes after about 90 minutes. In narcolepsy it often occurs within 15 minutes of falling asleep.
125172.m: In narcolepsy, REM sleep comes unusually early.

125173.q: What are vivid, dream-like sensations when falling asleep called, which are common in narcolepsy?
125173.e: Hypnagogic hallucinations occur during the transition from waking to sleeping. They arise because elements of REM sleep intrude into the waking state.
125173.m: Hypnagogic hallucinations occur when falling asleep.

125174.q: What is the experience called of briefly being unable to move a single muscle on waking, while fully conscious?
125174.e: In sleep paralysis, the muscle paralysis of REM sleep lasts briefly after waking up. It is more common in narcolepsy, but also happens to healthy people.
125174.m: In sleep paralysis you are awake but briefly unable to move.

125175.q: After which vaccination campaign was a rise in narcolepsy cases observed in some countries?
125175.e: Especially in Scandinavia, more cases of narcolepsy occurred after the swine flu vaccine Pandemrix. An autoimmune reaction in genetically susceptible people is suspected.
125175.m: After the 2009 swine flu vaccination, more narcolepsy cases occurred in some countries.

125176.q: What are people with an early chronotype called in everyday language?
125176.e: Larks wake up early and get tired early. Owls, on the other hand, are active late and like to sleep in.
125176.m: Larks are awake early, owls are active late.

125177.q: What does the term chronotype describe?
a: Whether someone tends to be active early or late
How long someone can hold their breath
125177.e: The chronotype describes your personal body clock. Larks are awake early, owls only really come alive in the evening.
125177.m: The chronotype describes whether you are an early riser or a night person.

125178.q: On which days does your own chronotype show most clearly?
a: On free days without an alarm clock
On school days with an early alarm
On days after a long journey
125178.e: Without an alarm, you sleep according to your own body clock. That is why researchers use sleep times on free days to determine the chronotype.
125178.m: Free days without an alarm show your true chronotype.

125179.q: At what age is the average person's chronotype at its latest?
125179.e: During adolescence, the chronotype shifts later and later. Around the age of 20 it is at its latest and then slowly becomes earlier again.
125179.m: Around the age of twenty, people have their latest chronotype.

125180.q: How does the chronotype typically change in later adulthood?
a: It stays exactly the same from age 20.
125180.e: On average, older people go to bed earlier and wake up earlier. This reflects the body clock shifting earlier.
125180.m: In old age the chronotype becomes earlier.

125181.q: Which external stimulus sets the human body clock most strongly?
125181.e: Light in the morning resets the body clock every day. People who get a lot of light in the evening and little in the morning tend to become late chronotypes.
125181.m: Light is the most important time cue for the body clock.

125182.q: What is the disorder called in which someone can only ever fall asleep and wake up very late?
125182.e: In delayed sleep phase syndrome, the body clock is shifted much later. Those affected often only fall asleep after midnight and find it hard to get out of bed in the morning.
125182.m: In delayed sleep phase syndrome, the body clock is shifted much later.

125183.q: Among other things, what does a person's chronotype depend on?
a: Only on the month they were born
125183.e: Twin and family studies show that the chronotype is partly inherited. Age and light also play a big role.

125184.q: What is meant by social jet lag?
a: The difference in mid-sleep time between working days and free days
Lack of sleep after a party
The time difference between two countries
125184.e: With social jet lag, the body clock has to live against its own rhythm because of school or work. At the weekend it then returns to its later times.
125184.m: Social jet lag happens when social schedules and the body clock do not match.

125185.q: On average, who is particularly affected by social jet lag?
125185.e: Teenagers have a late chronotype but have to go to school early. This gap between body clock and timetable is especially large for them.
125185.m: Teenagers suffer particularly often from social jet lag.

125186.q: A person sleeps from 11 pm to 6.30 am on working days and from 1 am to 10 am on free days. How big is their social jet lag?
125186.e: The mid-sleep point on working days is at 2.45 am, on free days at 5.30 am. The difference is 2 hours 45 minutes.
125186.m: Social jet lag is calculated from the difference between the two mid-sleep points.

125187.q: Someone sleeps from midnight to 7 am during the week and from 2 am to 11 am at the weekend. How big is the social jet lag?
125187.e: The mid-sleep point is at 3.30 am during the week and at 6.30 am at the weekend. The difference is 3 hours.
125187.m: For social jet lag you compare the mid-sleep points, not the length of sleep.

125188.q: Why do many people sleep much longer at the weekend than during the week?
a: They are catching up on sleep lost during the week.
The night is astronomically longer at the weekend.
The body basically needs twice as much sleep at the weekend.
Caffeine does not work at the weekend.
125188.e: During the week, the alarm clock shortens sleep, because you have to get up early despite a late body clock. At the weekend the sleep debt is partly made up.
125188.m: Sleeping in for a long time at the weekend often shows a sleep debt.

125189.q: Which health risk has social jet lag been linked to in studies?
a: An increased risk of being overweight
125189.e: Observational studies found that people with large social jet lag more often had a higher body mass index. Mood and performance can also suffer.
125189.m: Large social jet lag is more often linked to being overweight.

125190.q: Which measure can help reduce the social jet lag of a late chronotype?
a: Plenty of daylight in the morning
Bright screen light late in the evening
Sleeping until midday at the weekend
Drinking lots of coffee in the evening
125190.e: Morning light shifts the body clock earlier, so you get tired earlier in the evening. Light in the evening has the opposite effect.
125190.m: Morning light helps to set the body clock earlier.

125191.q: Which system in the brain does a job that the lymphatic system does in the rest of the body?
125191.e: The brain has no classic lymphatic vessels in its tissue. Instead, the glymphatic system, described in 2012, flushes out waste with brain fluid.
125191.m: The glymphatic system is the brain's rubbish collection.

125192.q: Where does the name “glymphatic” come from?
125192.e: The system depends on glial cells and does a job in the brain that the lymphatic system does elsewhere. The made-up word comes from this.
125192.m: The name glymphatic combines glial cells and the lymphatic system.

125193.q: What main job is attributed to the glymphatic system?
a: Flushing waste out of the brain
Producing hormones in the pituitary gland
Carrying nerve signals to the muscles
125193.e: Brain fluid flows through the tissue and carries away metabolic waste. In this way the brain is cleaned, even though it has no classic lymphatic vessels in its tissue.
125193.m: The glymphatic system flushes waste out of the brain.

125194.q: According to studies in mice, when does the glymphatic system work hardest?
125194.e: During sleep, the space between the brain cells gets much larger. This lets the fluid flow through the tissue much more easily.
125194.m: The brain is cleaned especially well during sleep.

125195.q: Which fluid flows through the brain tissue in the glymphatic system?
125195.e: Cerebrospinal fluid flows along the blood vessels into the tissue and mixes with the fluid between the cells. It then leaves the brain along the veins.
125195.m: In the glymphatic system, cerebrospinal fluid flows through the brain.

125196.q: Along which structures does brain fluid flow into the brain tissue in the glymphatic system?
125196.e: Brain fluid flows into the tissue in spaces around the arteries. Waste then leaves the brain along the veins.
125196.m: The glymphatic system uses the spaces around the blood vessels.

125197.q: Which cells form the walls of the channels along the blood vessels in the glymphatic system with their extensions?
125197.e: Astrocytes are glial cells that surround the blood vessels with their end feet. They form the outer boundary of the spaces in which the cerebrospinal fluid flows.
125197.m: Astrocytes wrap around the blood vessels of the brain.

125198.q: Which waste substance linked to Alzheimer's disease is removed by the glymphatic system?
125198.e: In Alzheimer's disease, beta-amyloid builds up as plaques. Studies show that more of it is washed out during sleep.
125198.m: The glymphatic system also removes beta-amyloid from the brain.

125199.q: Which bedroom temperature is usually recommended for a good night's sleep?
125199.e: As you fall asleep, your body temperature drops slightly. A fairly cool room supports this process.
125199.m: A cool bedroom helps you sleep well.

125200.q: How does alcohol in the evening affect sleep?
a: It makes falling asleep easier but disturbs sleep later on.
It improves sleep all night long.
It has no effect on sleep at all.
125200.e: Alcohol has a calming effect at first, but it suppresses REM sleep. In the second half of the night, sleep becomes restless and you wake up more often.
125200.m: Alcohol makes you tired but makes your sleep worse.

125201.q: Which rule about sleep times is one of the most important sleep hygiene recommendations?
a: Regular times for going to bed and getting up, even at the weekend
Going to bed at a different time every day
Sleeping until the afternoon at the weekend if possible
Only going to bed when completely exhausted
125201.e: Fixed times stabilise the body clock. Big differences between weekdays and the weekend throw the rhythm into confusion.
125201.m: Regular sleep times strengthen the body clock.

125202.q: What is the method called in which the bed is only used for sleeping, so that it becomes linked with sleep again?
125202.e: In stimulus control, the bed should not be used for working, eating or watching TV. This way the brain learns to connect bed and sleep again.
125202.m: In stimulus control, the bed is used only for sleeping.

125203.q: What is recommended if you cannot fall asleep after about 20 minutes in bed?
a: Get up and do something calm until you feel tired
Stay lying there and look at the clock
125203.e: Lying awake and brooding for a long time links the bed with being awake. It is better to get up and only go back when you feel sleepy.
125203.m: If you cannot fall asleep, it is better to get up for a while.

125204.q: What is true about sport in connection with good sleep?
a: Regular exercise helps, but intense sport just before sleeping tends not to.
