125675.q: Which quantity did Einstein add to his field equations in 1917 to allow a static universe?
125675.e: Einstein added the cosmological constant Λ to his equations. After the expansion of the universe was discovered he dropped it; today it is used to describe dark energy.
125675.m: The cosmological constant was introduced by Einstein and later rediscovered.

125676.q: When were gravitational waves detected directly for the first time?
125676.e: On 14 September 2015, the LIGO detectors in the USA recorded a signal. The discovery was announced in February 2016.
125676.m: Gravitational waves were measured directly for the first time in 2015.

125677.q: Which event produced the first directly measured gravitational waves?
a: The merger of two black holes
125677.e: Two black holes of about 30 solar masses each orbited each other and merged. Part of their mass was radiated away as gravitational waves.
125677.m: The first signal came from two merging black holes.

125678.q: At what speed do gravitational waves travel?
a: At half the speed of light
125678.e: According to general relativity, disturbances of spacetime travel at the speed of light. Observations have confirmed this very precisely.
125678.m: Gravitational waves are as fast as light.

125679.q: How do detectors such as LIGO measure gravitational waves?
a: With laser interferometers that detect tiny changes in length
With huge telescope mirrors for visible light
125679.e: A gravitational wave alternately squeezes and stretches the arms, which are kilometres long. The change in length is much smaller than the diameter of a proton and is measured using light interference.
125679.m: Gravitational wave detectors measure tiny changes in length with laser light.

125680.q: Who predicted the existence of gravitational waves in theory?
125680.e: Shortly after completing his theory of gravity, Einstein worked out that disturbances of spacetime spread as waves. He himself thought they could hardly be measured.

125681.q: Which observation provided indirect evidence of gravitational waves even before 2015?
a: The shrinking orbit of a binary pulsar
125681.e: Russell Hulse and Joseph Taylor discovered a binary pulsar whose orbital period decreases exactly as the emission of gravitational waves requires. They received the Nobel Prize for this in 1993.
125681.m: A binary pulsar provided the first indirect evidence of gravitational waves.

125682.q: What is the name of ESA’s planned gravitational wave observatory in space?
125682.e: LISA is to consist of three satellites millions of kilometres apart. LIGO, Virgo and KAGRA, by contrast, are detectors on Earth.
125682.m: LISA is meant to measure gravitational waves in space.

125683.q: What is the typical signal of two merging objects called, whose frequency and strength rise rapidly just before the merger?
125683.e: The closer the two bodies get, the faster they orbit each other. Turned into sound, the signal is like a rising twitter, a “chirp”.
125683.m: Merging objects produce a rising chirp signal.

125684.q: How does a gravitational wave deform the space it passes through?
a: It stretches and squeezes it at right angles to the direction of travel
It only stretches it in the direction of travel
It does not change it at all
125684.e: Gravitational waves are transverse waves. At right angles to the direction of travel, space is alternately stretched in one direction and squeezed in the other.
125684.m: Gravitational waves stretch and squeeze space at right angles to their direction of travel.

125685.q: Which astrophysicist found a solution of the field equations in 1916 that sets the radius of a non-rotating black hole?
125685.e: Karl Schwarzschild found the solution shortly after Einstein’s publication. The radius named after him is r = 2GM/c².
125685.m: The Schwarzschild radius describes the size of a black hole.

125686.q: Which project published the first image of a black hole in 2019?
125686.e: The Event Horizon Telescope links radio telescopes all over the Earth into one giant virtual telescope. The image shows the shadow of the black hole in the galaxy M87.
125686.m: The Event Horizon Telescope produced the first image of a black hole.

125687.q: What is the name of the supermassive black hole at the centre of the Milky Way?
125687.e: Sagittarius A* lies in the constellation Sagittarius and has about four million solar masses. The orbits of nearby stars revealed its mass.
125687.m: At the centre of the Milky Way is the black hole Sagittarius A*.

125688.q: According to a prediction from quantum theory, which radiation should black holes emit?
125688.e: Stephen Hawking showed that black holes should radiate weakly because of quantum effects at the horizon. As a result, they could evaporate over an extremely long time.
125688.m: According to Hawking, black holes should radiate weakly.

125689.q: How do stellar black holes form?
a: Through the collapse of a very massive star
Through the explosion of a planet
Through the cooling of a white dwarf
125689.e: When a very massive star has used up its fuel, its core collapses under its own gravity. This is often preceded by a supernova.
125689.m: Stellar black holes form from collapsing massive stars.

125690.q: What is the stretching of a body by extreme tidal forces near a black hole called?
125690.e: The pull on the nearer part of a body is much stronger than on the farther part. As a result, the body is stretched lengthways and squeezed from the sides.
125690.m: Tidal forces can stretch bodies near a black hole.

125691.q: What is the rotating disc of gas and dust that spirals into a black hole called?
125691.e: The inflowing matter forms a flat, rotating disc and heats up strongly through friction. That is why the surroundings of a black hole often shine brightly.
125691.m: Matter flows into a black hole through an accretion disc.

125692.q: According to the so-called no-hair theorem, which three quantities completely describe a black hole?
a: Mass, angular momentum and electric charge
125692.e: All other properties of the matter that has fallen in are lost to the outside. Only mass, angular momentum and charge remain.
125692.m: A black hole is determined solely by mass, angular momentum and charge.

125693.q: What is the boundary around a black hole called, beyond which not even light can escape?
125693.e: Inside the event horizon, you would have to be faster than light to escape. That is why no information gets out from there.
125693.m: Nothing escapes from inside the event horizon of a black hole.

125694.q: According to special relativity, how does the high orbital speed affect the clocks of GPS satellites?
a: They run about 7 microseconds slower per day
They run about 7 seconds slower per day
They run about 7 microseconds faster per day
125694.e: The satellites move at almost 4 kilometres per second. Because of time dilation, their clocks lose about 7 microseconds per day.
125694.m: The orbital speed makes GPS clocks run slower.

125695.q: According to general relativity, how does the weaker gravity at orbital height affect GPS clocks?
a: They run about 45 microseconds faster per day
They run about 45 microseconds slower per day
They run about 45 seconds faster per day
125695.e: Farther from the Earth, the gravitational field is weaker and time passes faster. The effect amounts to about 45 microseconds per day.
125695.m: At height, clocks run faster because of the weaker gravity.

125696.q: Which relativistic effect dominates for the clocks of GPS satellites?
a: The gravitational effect; the clocks run fast overall
The speed effect; the clocks run slow overall
Both cancel each other out exactly
125696.e: The orbital speed slows the satellite clocks down, while the weaker gravity speeds them up. At a height of about 20,000 km the gravitational effect is much larger, so the clocks run fast overall.
125696.m: With GPS, the gravitational effect dominates and the satellite clocks run fast.

125697.q: Without relativistic correction, roughly how large would the position error grow after one day?
125697.e: The satellite clocks run about 38 microseconds fast per day overall; multiplied by the speed of light, that gives 38 · 10⁻⁶ s · 3 · 10⁸ m/s ≈ 11,400 m. Without correction, GPS would be useless after a short time.
125697.m: Without relativity, GPS would be kilometres out after one day.

125698.q: How are the relativistic effects corrected for GPS satellites?
a: The clock frequency is set slightly lower before launch
The satellites are brought back to Earth every day
125698.e: The base frequency of the satellite clocks is reduced so that, in orbit, they run correctly as seen from the Earth. Receivers calculate further small corrections themselves.
125698.m: GPS clocks are adjusted for relativistic effects before launch.

125699.q: A GPS signal travels for about 0.07 seconds. Why does the Earth’s rotation have to be taken into account?
a: The receiver moves on with the Earth during this time
The Earth’s rotation slows the radio signal down
The Earth’s rotation changes the frequency of the atomic clocks
Otherwise the satellites would stand still
125699.e: While the signal is on its way, the receiver turns a little further with the Earth. At the equator this is over 30 metres, which would distort the position.
125699.m: With GPS, the Earth’s rotation during the signal’s travel time must also be corrected.

125700.q: Which European satellite navigation system also has to be corrected for relativity?
125700.e: Galileo is operated by the European Union and also uses atomic clocks in orbit. The same relativistic effects act on all such systems.
125700.m: The European Galileo system also needs relativistic corrections.

125701.q: Which relativistic correction does the GPS receiver calculate itself, because it changes during the orbit?
a: The correction for the slightly elliptical orbit
The correction for the lunar cycle
125701.e: On a slightly elliptical orbit, the satellite’s height and speed change periodically. As a result, the rate of its clock also varies, and the receiver corrects this by calculation.
125701.m: The shape of the satellites’ orbits requires an extra correction in the receiver.

125702.q: During which period did Albert Einstein live in today’s Einstein House in Bern?
125702.e: Einstein lived in the flat during his productive years in Bern. Several of his groundbreaking papers were written during this time.
125702.m: Einstein lived on the Kramgasse from 1903 to 1905.

125703.q: Which museum in Bern has its own permanent exhibition on Einstein’s life, in addition to the Einstein House?
125703.e: The Einstein Museum is part of the Bern Historical Museum. It presents Einstein’s life and work in detail.
125703.m: The Einstein Museum is in the Bern Historical Museum.

125704.q: Which famous theory did Einstein publish in 1905, while he was living in Bern?
125704.e: 1905 is considered Einstein’s miracle year. In Bern he wrote, among other things, the paper on special relativity while working at the patent office.
125704.m: Einstein developed special relativity in Bern.

125705.q: Which famous Bern landmark stands at the top end of the Kramgasse, just a few steps from the Einstein House?
125705.e: The Kramgasse leads from the Zytglogge towards the Nydegg Bridge. The medieval clock tower is one of the city’s best-known buildings.
125705.m: The Zytglogge is very close to the Einstein House.

125706.q: To which UNESCO World Heritage Site does the building housing the Einstein House belong?
125706.e: The Einstein House is right in the middle of Bern’s Old City with its arcades and fountains. The Old City as a whole is on the UNESCO World Heritage List.
125706.m: The Einstein House is in the UNESCO World Heritage Site of the Old City of Bern.

125707.q: On what occasion was Einstein’s former flat in Bern opened as a museum?
125707.e: The flat was opened as a museum on 14 March 1979, Einstein’s hundredth birthday. Since then, people from all over the world have visited the small museum.
125707.m: The Einstein House was opened for Einstein’s 100th birthday.

125708.q: Which fountain with a figure stands in the Kramgasse, the street where the Einstein House is?
125708.e: The Zähringer Fountain shows a bear in armour and recalls the founders of the city, the Dukes of Zähringen. The other fountains stand in other streets and squares of the Old City.
125708.m: The Zähringer Fountain stands in the Kramgasse.

125709.q: Which fundamental change is at the centre of the Neolithic Revolution?
a: The move to farming crops and keeping animals
The move to a culture of writing
The move to sailing the open seas
125709.e: People gradually gave up living as hunter-gatherers and produced their own food. This went together with settling down, storing supplies and new kinds of settlement.
125709.m: In the Neolithic Revolution, people became farmers and herders.

125710.q: Roughly when did the Neolithic Revolution begin in the Near East?
125710.e: At the end of the last Ice Age, about 12,000 years ago, people in the Near East began to use and grow wild cereals on purpose. In central Europe, farming only began thousands of years later.
125710.m: Farming began in the Near East about 12,000 years ago.

125711.q: Why is the site of Göbekli Tepe in Turkey so important for research?
a: Monumental buildings probably made by hunter-gatherers
The first royal tomb with written finds
The oldest known harbour on the Mediterranean
125711.e: The stone circles with T-shaped pillars were built about 11,000 years ago, apparently before fully developed farming. This challenges the idea that large buildings were only possible after people settled down.
125711.m: Göbekli Tepe shows that even hunter-gatherers built monuments.

125712.q: Which health consequence did the farming way of life of the Neolithic often bring?
a: More diseases passed on from animals
Less tooth decay because of the grain
125712.e: Living closely with domestic animals and in crowded settlements favoured zoonoses. Skeletons of early farmers also often show more tooth decay and a smaller body height than those of hunter-gatherers.
125712.m: Early farmers suffered more often from diseases that came from animals.

125713.q: Why did farming encourage social differences in society?
a: Hunting prey was shared out more evenly
Settlements became smaller and more mobile
125713.e: Harvest surpluses that could be stored could be piled up and shared out. This led to differences in wealth, specialised jobs and later elites.
125713.m: Harvest surpluses made differences in wealth and specialisation possible.

125714.q: Which settlement in central Anatolia is considered one of the largest settlements of the Neolithic?
125714.e: About 9,000 years ago, Çatalhöyük was home to several thousand people. The houses stood close together and were entered through the roofs.
125714.m: Çatalhöyük is one of the largest settlements of the Neolithic.

125715.q: Which tool is typical of the Neolithic and was used to clear forest?
125715.e: With polished stone axes in wooden handles, the first farmers cleared forest for fields and houses. Polished stone tools are a hallmark of the Neolithic.
125715.m: The first farmers cleared forest with polished stone axes.

125716.q: Why is the area from the Persian Gulf to the Levant called the “Fertile Crescent”?
a: The fertile land curves in an arc round the Syrian Desert
The moon looks especially big there
The fields were laid out in the shape of a crescent
The area belonged to the Ottoman Empire, whose symbol was the crescent
125716.e: On the map, the fertile river valleys and hill country form an arc round the desert. One of the first kinds of farming arose there about 11,000 years ago.
125716.m: The Fertile Crescent is an arc of fertile land round the Syrian Desert.

125717.q: Which two rivers shape the eastern part of the Fertile Crescent?
125717.e: The Euphrates and Tigris flow through Mesopotamia, the “land between the rivers”. Their water later made large irrigation cultures possible.
125717.m: The Euphrates and Tigris form the heart of Mesopotamia.

125718.q: Which present-day country does NOT lie in the area of the Fertile Crescent?
125718.e: The Fertile Crescent stretches from the Levant through south-eastern Anatolia to Mesopotamia and the Persian Gulf. The Arabian Peninsula with its deserts is not part of it.
125718.m: The Fertile Crescent curves round the Syrian Desert to the north.

125719.q: Which cereal is one of the first crops of the Fertile Crescent?
125719.e: Barley, einkorn and emmer were the first to be domesticated in the Near East. Maize comes from America, while rice and millet were mainly grown in Asia and Africa.
125719.m: Barley is one of the oldest cereals of the Near East.

125720.q: Which pulse is one of the founder crops of the Fertile Crescent?
125720.e: Lentils, peas and chickpeas were domesticated in the Near East. The soya bean comes from East Asia, and the peanut and common bean from America.
125720.m: The lentil is one of the oldest crops of the Near East.

125721.q: Which farm animals were first domesticated in the area of the Fertile Crescent?
125721.e: Sheep and goats became domestic animals in Anatolia and the Zagros Mountains about 10,000 years ago or earlier. Llamas and alpacas come from the Andes, the horse from the steppes of Eurasia.
125721.m: Sheep and goats are among the first farm animals of the Near East.

125722.q: Which feature of the wild plants in the Fertile Crescent made early farming easier?
125722.e: The climate with wet winters and dry summers favoured annual plants with large seeds that could be stored. The geographer Jared Diamond saw this as one reason for early farming in this region.
125722.m: Large-seeded annual wild grasses made it easier to start farming.

125723.q: Which mountain range forms the eastern edge of the Fertile Crescent?
125723.e: The Zagros Mountains in present-day Iran and Iraq form the eastern edge. Very early evidence of goat keeping has been found in their foothills.
125723.m: The Zagros Mountains form the eastern edge of the Fertile Crescent.

125724.q: Which animal is considered the oldest domestic animal of humans?
125724.e: The dog descends from the wolf and was domesticated even before farming was invented. Estimates go back more than 15,000 years.
125724.m: The dog is humans’ oldest domestic animal.

125725.q: Which feature is typical of domesticated cereals compared with the wild form?
a: Ripe ears no longer fall apart
The seeds are scattered far and wide
125725.e: In wild cereals, the stalk of the ear breaks when ripe so that the seeds fall out. Without meaning to, farmers mainly harvested plants with a firm stalk and sowed them again.
125725.m: Domesticated cereals keep their grains in the ripe ear.

125726.q: What is the whole set of features called that distinguishes crops from their wild forms?
125726.e: The domestication syndrome includes, for example, larger seeds, ripening at the same time and the loss of natural seed dispersal. Similar changes appeared independently in many crops.
125726.m: The domestication syndrome sums up typical features of crops.

125727.q: Which wild cat is considered the ancestor of the domestic cat?
125727.e: Genetic studies show that the domestic cat descends from the African wildcat (Felis lybica) of North Africa and the Near East. Cats probably joined the first farmers because mice were attracted to the grain stores.
125727.m: The domestic cat descends from the African wildcat.

125728.q: Which naturalist published a work in 1868 on the variation of animals and plants under domestication?
125728.e: In “The Variation of Animals and Plants under Domestication”, Darwin described the changes in domestic animals and crops. He used artificial selection as a model for natural selection.
125728.m: Darwin used breeding as a model for natural selection.

125729.q: According to current knowledge, where was rice of the subspecies japonica domesticated?
a: In the Yangtze valley in China
In the Nile valley in Egypt
125729.e: Archaeological and genetic findings point to the Yangtze area in China. There, wild rice turned into cultivated rice over thousands of years.
125729.m: Rice was domesticated on the Yangtze in China.

125730.q: Why could many crops hardly survive without humans?
a: They no longer spread their seeds themselves
125730.e: A maize cob, for example, does not drop its grains; if it germinates as a whole, the seedlings compete crowded together. In crops, humans take over seed dispersal.
125730.m: Many crops depend on humans to sow them.

125731.q: What is the deliberate selection by humans of animals and plants for further breeding called?
125731.e: In artificial selection, humans decide which individuals reproduce. Over generations, desired features become stronger.
125731.m: In artificial selection, humans choose the animals and plants for breeding.

125732.q: How many sets of chromosomes does einkorn have?
125732.e: Einkorn is diploid with 14 chromosomes. It is therefore considered the genetically simplest of the cultivated wheat species.
125732.m: Einkorn is the diploid wheat species.

125733.q: In which region was einkorn domesticated, like the other early cereals?
a: In the Fertile Crescent in the Near East
In the Yangtze valley in China
In the Po Valley in northern Italy
125733.e: Genetic comparisons point to the Karacadağ mountains in south-eastern Turkey. They lie in the northern Fertile Crescent, where farming began over 10,000 years ago.
125733.m: Einkorn comes from the Fertile Crescent.

125734.q: In which famous find was einkorn shown to be part of the last meal?
125734.e: In the stomach of the glacier mummy, which is about 5,300 years old, researchers found remains of einkorn and game meat, among other things. Ötzi lived in the late Neolithic.
125734.m: Ötzi had eaten einkorn before he died.

125735.q: Why is einkorn one of the hulled cereals?
a: The grains stay enclosed when threshed
It only grows on marshy soils
It is only used as animal feed
125735.e: In hulled cereals, the grains are still held tightly in their husks after threshing. They have to be dehulled in an extra step.
125735.m: Hulled cereals have to be dehulled after threshing.

125736.q: What is the scientific name of cultivated einkorn?
125736.e: “Monococcum” roughly means “single-grained”. Triticum aestivum is bread wheat, Triticum durum is durum wheat and Hordeum vulgare is barley.
125736.m: The scientific name of einkorn is Triticum monococcum.

125737.q: What colour is einkorn flour because of its high carotenoid content?
125737.e: Einkorn contains a lot of lutein, a yellow pigment from the carotenoid group. That is why flour and pasta made from einkorn are strikingly yellow.
125737.m: Einkorn flour is yellowish because of its carotenoids.

125738.q: Why is einkorn hardly grown on a large scale any more?
a: It gives a much smaller yield than bread wheat
Growing it is banned in Europe
125738.e: Einkorn has small grains, has to be dehulled and gives a much smaller yield than modern wheat. Today it is grown again in small amounts for speciality products.
125738.m: Einkorn gives a low yield and has therefore become rare.

125739.q: How many grains does a spikelet of emmer typically contain?
125739.e: Emmer usually forms two grains per spikelet and is therefore also called “Zweikorn” (two-grain) in German. It is one of the oldest kinds of wheat.
125739.m: Emmer usually has two grains per spikelet.

125740.q: Which kind of wheat developed from emmer and is used today mainly for pasta?
125740.e: Durum wheat (Triticum durum), like emmer, is tetraploid and developed from cultivated emmer. Its grains can be threshed free of their husks.
125740.m: Durum wheat for pasta descends from emmer.

125741.q: How did hexaploid bread wheat, from which most bread is baked today, come about?
a: By a cross between a tetraploid wheat and a wild grass
By a cross between rye and barley
By targeted genetic engineering in the 20th century
By doubling the chromosomes of maize
125741.e: About 8,000 years ago, tetraploid cultivated wheat crossed by chance with a goat grass. A third set of chromosomes was added, and hexaploid bread wheat was the result.
125741.m: Bread wheat came from a cross between wheat and a wild grass.

125742.q: In which region was emmer first grown?
a: In the foothills of the Alps
125742.e: Wild emmer grows in the Near East. There, about 10,000 years ago, it became one of the first crops.
125742.m: Emmer comes from the Fertile Crescent.

125743.q: In which ancient civilisation was emmer the most important wheat?
125743.e: In Ancient Egypt, bread and beer were made from emmer. Finds from tombs show how important it was.
125743.m: In Ancient Egypt, emmer was the most important wheat.

125744.q: How many sets of chromosomes does emmer have?
125744.e: Emmer combines the chromosome sets of two wild grass species and is therefore tetraploid. Its genome includes 28 chromosomes.
125744.m: Emmer is a tetraploid wheat species.

125745.q: Which kind of wheat is called “Zweikorn” (two-grain) in German because it has two grains per spikelet?
125745.e: Emmer usually forms two grains per spikelet. Einkorn has only one, while spelt and durum wheat are other forms of wheat.
125745.m: Emmer usually has two grains per spikelet.

125746.q: What is the formation of a species by combining the chromosome sets of two different species called, as in emmer?
125746.e: Wild emmer came from a cross between Triticum urartu and a goat grass, in which the chromosome sets of both parents were kept. In autopolyploidy, by contrast, the set of the same species is multiplied.
125746.m: Allopolyploidy combines the chromosome sets of different species.

125747.q: Which wild plant does maize descend from?
125747.e: Genetic studies show that maize developed from a subspecies of teosinte. Although they are closely related, the plants look very different.

125748.q: In which present-day country was maize domesticated from teosinte?
125748.e: Domestication took place in the south of present-day Mexico. From there, maize spread across the whole of America.
125748.m: Maize was domesticated in present-day Mexico.

125749.q: How did teosinte turn into today’s maize over time?
a: Through a single cross with wheat
Through genetic engineering in the 20th century
125749.e: Over many generations, farmers chose plants with larger grains that were easier to harvest. This artificial selection changed teosinte step by step into maize.
125749.m: Maize is the result of long selection by humans.

125750.q: Roughly how long ago was maize domesticated?
125750.e: Genetic dating and finds of starch grains point to a start about 9,000 years ago. Large cobs only developed over thousands of years.
125750.m: Maize was domesticated about 9,000 years ago.

125751.q: What finally confirmed that maize descends from teosinte?
125751.e: Genetic studies showed that maize is most closely related to a teosinte subspecies from Mexico. The Nobel Prize winner George Beadle had already argued for this origin.
125751.m: Genome comparisons confirmed that maize descends from teosinte.

125752.q: How do teosinte grains clearly differ from maize grains?
a: They are enclosed in a hard case
They are much bigger than maize grains
They sit on a thick cob
They are coloured blue and soft
125752.e: Teosinte grains are enclosed in a hard fruit case. A change in the gene tga1 exposed the grain in maize.
125752.m: Teosinte grains have a hard case, maize grains are exposed.

125753.q: How does the growth of teosinte differ from that of maize?
a: Teosinte is heavily branched, maize has one main stalk
Teosinte is a tree, maize a grass
Teosinte grows under water, maize on land
Teosinte climbs up trees, maize stands on its own
125753.e: Teosinte forms many side shoots. In maize, a change in the gene tb1 suppresses the side shoots, so that one strong main stalk forms.
125753.m: Maize grows unbranched, teosinte heavily branched.

125754.q: Roughly how many grains does an ear of teosinte carry?
125754.e: An ear of teosinte consists of a few grains lying one behind the other. A modern maize cob, on the other hand, carries several hundred grains.
125754.m: An ear of teosinte has only about a dozen grains or fewer.

125755.q: What is meant by the Columbian Exchange?
a: The exchange of plants, animals and diseases between America and the Old World
A trade agreement between Spain and Portugal
Swapping gold for spices in India
A prisoner exchange after the conquest of Mexico
125755.e: After 1492, potatoes and maize, for example, came to Europe, while horses, wheat and smallpox came to America. The historian Alfred W. Crosby coined the term in 1972.
125755.m: The Columbian Exchange linked the plants, animals and diseases of both worlds.

125756.q: Which plant came from America to Europe through the Columbian Exchange?
125756.e: The tomato comes from Central and South America and became known in Europe after 1492. Wheat, sugar cane and coffee travelled in the opposite direction.
125756.m: The tomato came from America to Europe.

125757.q: Which animal came from Europe to America and changed the lives of many peoples of the prairie?
125757.e: Horses had died out in America and came back with the Spanish. Many prairie peoples became bison hunters on horseback.
125757.m: The horse came back to America with the Europeans.

125758.q: What was the main cause of the massive population decline of the Indigenous peoples of America after 1492?
a: Crop failures caused by volcanic eruptions
Wars between the Incas and the Aztecs
125758.e: People in America had no resistance to smallpox, measles and flu. Epidemics killed a large part of the population, often even before direct contact with Europeans.
125758.m: Introduced epidemics devastated the Indigenous peoples of America.

125759.q: Which spice from America shapes Hungarian cooking today?
125759.e: Paprika belongs to the genus Capsicum from America and spread to Hungary via the Mediterranean region and the Ottoman Empire. Today it is seen as the national spice there.

125760.q: Which American root crop became a staple food in Africa?
125760.e: Cassava comes from South America and was brought to Africa by the Portuguese. Yams and taro, on the other hand, are plants of the Old World.
125760.m: Cassava came from South America to Africa.

125761.q: Which Old World plant was grown on plantations in the Caribbean and drove the transatlantic slave trade?
125761.e: Sugar cane comes from Asia and was grown on a huge scale in the Caribbean and Brazil. Millions of people were taken from Africa by force to work on the plantations.
125761.m: Growing sugar cane was closely linked with the slave trade.

125762.q: Where does the cocoa plant originally come from?
125762.e: Cocoa was already used in Mesoamerica by the Olmecs, Maya and Aztecs. West Africa is the largest producer today, but it is not the plant’s home.
125762.m: Cocoa comes from America, even though it mainly grows in West Africa today.

125763.q: Which bird came from America to Europe through the Columbian Exchange?
125763.e: The turkey was domesticated in Mexico and came to Europe in the 16th century. Chickens, guinea fowl and pheasants come from the Old World.

125764.q: In which fields did Nikolai Vavilov do research?
125764.e: Vavilov was a Russian botanist and geneticist. He studied the origin and diversity of crops.
125764.m: Nikolai Vavilov was a botanist and geneticist.

125765.q: What did Nikolai Vavilov discover about the origin of crops?
a: They come from a few centres of origin with great diversity
They arose everywhere in the world at the same time
They all descend from a single wild plant
125765.e: Vavilov found that there are regions where a crop and its wild relatives are especially diverse. That is probably where it was first grown.
125765.m: Crops come from a few centres of origin.

125766.q: Which opponent in Soviet biology contributed greatly to Vavilov’s persecution?
125766.e: Lysenko rejected classical genetics and had Stalin’s support. Vavilov was arrested in 1940.
125766.m: Lysenko’s influence led to Vavilov’s persecution.

125767.q: What did Nikolai Vavilov die of?
125767.e: Vavilov was sentenced to death, but the sentence was changed to imprisonment. He died in prison in 1943 as a result of hunger.
125767.m: Vavilov died of hunger as a prisoner.

125768.q: What did Nikolai Vavilov build up in Leningrad?
a: One of the largest seed collections in the world
The world’s first nuclear research centre
A museum of minerals and ores
125768.e: Vavilov’s institute collected seeds from all over the world to preserve the diversity of crops for breeding. The collection still exists in St Petersburg today.
125768.m: Vavilov created a huge seed collection.

125769.q: What did staff at Vavilov’s institute do during the Siege of Leningrad?
a: They went hungry rather than eat the seeds
They burnt the collection for heating
They sowed everything in the city parks
125769.e: Several staff members died of hunger, although they were guarding tonnes of edible seeds and tubers. They wanted to keep the collection for the future.
125769.m: The guardians of the seed collection stood firm even when starving.

125770.q: Under which Soviet ruler was Nikolai Vavilov arrested and sentenced?
125770.e: Vavilov was arrested under Stalin in 1940 because he defended classical genetics. He was only rehabilitated after Stalin’s death.

125771.q: Why did Nikolai Vavilov go on many research trips to lots of countries?
a: To collect seeds and wild forms
125771.e: On expeditions in Asia, Africa, Europe and America he collected crops and their wild relatives. These finds formed the basis of his theory.
125771.m: Vavilov collected plants worldwide on expeditions.

125772.q: What is meant by the gene centre of a crop?
a: The region with the greatest genetic diversity
A lab where genes are changed
An area where no crops grow
A part of the cell nucleus with many genes
125772.e: According to Vavilov, a crop’s diversity is greatest where it has been grown the longest. Gene centres are therefore often seen as regions of origin.
125772.m: In the gene centre, a crop’s genetic diversity is greatest.

125773.q: Why are gene centres important for plant breeding?
a: Wild relatives provide genes, for example for resistance
Plants grow there without any water
There are no pests or diseases there
All forms of breeding are banned there
125773.e: Gene centres have old local varieties and wild relatives with features that modern varieties lack. Breeders cross them in, for example for resistance to diseases.
125773.m: Gene centres are treasure chests for breeding.

125774.q: Which crop has its gene centre in the highlands of Ethiopia?
125774.e: Coffea arabica comes from the mountain forests of Ethiopia, where wild coffee plants still grow today. Vavilov counted Ethiopia among the important gene centres.

125775.q: Which crop comes from the East Asian gene centre in China?
125775.e: The soya bean was domesticated in north-eastern China. The chickpea comes from the Near East, the sunflower and potato from America.
125775.m: The soya bean comes from China.

125776.q: Where is the global seed vault that keeps seed samples from all over the world safe?
125776.e: The Svalbard Global Seed Vault lies in a mountain near Longyearbyen in the permafrost. It keeps backup copies from seed banks all over the world.
125776.m: The global seed vault is on Svalbard.

125777.q: Which Swiss foundation works to preserve old crop varieties and livestock breeds?
125777.e: ProSpecieRara preserves rare varieties and breeds by passing on seeds and animals to nurseries and farms. Pro Juventute, Pro Senectute and Pro Helvetia have other tasks.
125777.m: ProSpecieRara preserves old varieties and breeds in Switzerland.

125778.q: What is the loss of genetic diversity in crops and livestock called?
125778.e: When a few high-yield varieties push out old local varieties, genes are lost for ever. This process is called genetic erosion.
125778.m: Genetic erosion means the loss of genetic diversity.

125779.q: Where is the gene centre of the cultivated apple and its wild ancestor?
a: In the Tian Shan mountains of Central Asia
In the Alps of central Europe
125779.e: The wild apple Malus sieversii grows in the forests of the Tian Shan, for example in Kazakhstan. It is considered the most important ancestor of the cultivated apple.
125779.m: The cultivated apple comes from the Tian Shan in Central Asia.

125780.q: Since which year have the prehistoric pile dwellings around the Alps been a UNESCO World Heritage Site?
125780.e: In 2011, UNESCO added a selection of pile dwelling sites to the World Heritage List. Many of them are in Switzerland.
125780.m: The pile dwellings around the Alps have been World Heritage since 2011.

125781.q: In how many countries are the sites of the World Heritage “Prehistoric Pile Dwellings around the Alps”?
125781.e: The sites are in Switzerland, Germany, Austria, France, Italy and Slovenia. Of the 111 sites, 56 are in Switzerland, about half.
125781.m: The pile dwelling World Heritage is spread across six countries.

125782.q: Where were remains of pile dwellings spotted at low water in the winter of 1853/54, starting the “pile dwelling fever”?
125782.e: The low water level uncovered piles and finds in Obermeilen. After that, pile dwellings were discovered at many Swiss lakes.
125782.m: The find at Obermeilen on Lake Zurich started the pile dwelling fever.

125783.q: Which Zurich antiquarian interpreted the finds from Obermeilen as pile dwellings?
125783.e: Ferdinand Keller imagined villages on platforms above the water. His interpretation shaped the picture of the pile dwellers for a long time.
125783.m: Ferdinand Keller founded the pile dwelling theory.

125784.q: Why have especially many plant remains survived in pile dwelling settlements?
a: No air in the wet lake bed
A dry climate like in the desert
125784.e: In waterlogged ground there is no oxygen, so wood, seeds and textiles hardly rot. That is why wetland settlements provide lots of evidence of early farming.
125784.m: The oxygen-poor lake bed preserves plant remains.

125785.q: Which method can often date wood from pile dwelling settlements to the exact year?
125785.e: Dendrochronology compares the tree-ring pattern of a piece of wood with a reference curve. This often makes it possible to find the year a tree was felled.
125785.m: Tree rings reveal the year the pile dwelling wood was felled.

125786.q: Which fibre plant did the pile dwellers grow for cords and textiles?
125786.e: Flax seeds, fibres and remains of fabric have been found in pile dwelling settlements. Flax provided both fibres and oily seeds.
125786.m: The pile dwellers used flax for textiles.

125787.q: How does modern research correct the romantic picture of pile dwellings?
a: Many houses stood on shores that were flooded at times
The houses floated on large rafts
The villages were only lived in during winter
The piles were carved from stone
125787.e: Many settlements lay on the shore, which flooded during high water. The houses were therefore raised on piles, but did not stand in the middle of the lake.
125787.m: Many pile dwellings stood on the lakeshore and not in open water.

125788.q: Which archaeology museum in Hauterive (NE) shows important finds from pile dwelling settlements?
125788.e: The Laténium on Lake Neuchâtel is one of the largest archaeology museums in Switzerland. It also shows finds from the lakeshore settlements.
125788.m: The Laténium in Hauterive shows pile dwelling finds.

125789.q: Which group of islands in Indonesia was known as the “Spice Islands”?
125789.e: Cloves and nutmegs grew on the Moluccas and were highly prized in Europe. The struggle for these islands shaped colonial history.
125789.m: The Moluccas are the famous Spice Islands.

125790.q: On which coast of India was the most important growing area for black pepper?
125790.e: Black pepper comes from the humid forests of the Malabar Coast in south-west India. Ports such as Calicut and Cochin were therefore the goal of European sailors.
125790.m: Pepper comes from the Malabar Coast in south-west India.

125791.q: Which city controlled a large part of the spice trade with the Levant in the late Middle Ages?
125791.e: Venetian merchants bought spices in Alexandria and Beirut and sold them on all over Europe. This trade made Venice rich.
125791.m: Venice became rich through the spice trade.

125792.q: Which trading company was founded in 1602 and soon controlled the spice trade with Indonesia?
125792.e: The Dutch VOC was given wide-ranging rights, for example to wage war. It gained a monopoly on nutmeg and cloves.
125792.m: The Dutch VOC controlled the trade in nutmeg and cloves.

125793.q: From which part of the plant is saffron obtained?
a: From the stigmas of the crocus flower
From the roots of the crocus
From the seeds of the crocus
From the corm of the crocus
125793.e: Each flower of Crocus sativus gives only three stigma threads, which are picked by hand. That is why saffron is one of the most expensive spices.
125793.m: Saffron consists of the stigmas of the saffron crocus.

125794.q: Which spice is obtained from the bark of a tree and used to come mainly from Sri Lanka?
125794.e: Ceylon cinnamon consists of the dried inner bark of the cinnamon tree. The island was for a long time the most important place it came from.

125795.q: Which small nutmeg island did the Dutch keep in the Treaty of Breda in 1667, while England kept New Amsterdam?
125795.e: The island of Run belongs to the Banda Islands, the home of the nutmeg. New Amsterdam later became a world city as New York.
125795.m: For the nutmeg island of Run, the Dutch gave up New Amsterdam.

125796.q: Who was mockingly called a “pepper sack” (German “Pfeffersack”) in the late Middle Ages?
125796.e: Pepper was so expensive that traders made great fortunes from it. The nickname mocked their wealth.
125796.m: A “pepper sack” was a rich merchant.

125797.q: Which spice from Mexico is grown today mainly on Madagascar, where it is pollinated by hand?
125797.e: Outside Mexico, the natural pollinators of the vanilla orchid are missing. That is why every flower has to be pollinated by hand, which makes vanilla very expensive.
125797.m: Outside Mexico, vanilla has to be pollinated by hand.

125798.q: What are the potatoes of the Andean peoples called that are preserved by frost and sun?
125798.e: The tubers are left out in the frost at night, dried during the day and squeezed. This way chuño keeps for years and was an important supply in the Inca Empire.
125798.m: Chuño is an ancient way of preserving potatoes.

125799.q: Who first brought the potato to Europe in the 16th century?
125799.e: The Spanish brought the tuber from South America in the second half of the 16th century. At first it was seen in many places as a botanical curiosity.
125799.m: The Spanish brought the potato to Europe.

125800.q: Which Prussian king promoted potato growing in 1756 with the so-called “Potato Order”?
125800.e: Frederick II, known as Frederick the Great, ordered the potato to be grown in order to prevent famines. Many farmers were suspicious of the new plant at first.
125800.m: Frederick the Great promoted the potato in Prussia.

125801.q: Which French pharmacist made the potato popular in France?
125801.e: In the 18th century, Parmentier promoted the potato with experiments and banquets. Several potato dishes still bear his name today.
125801.m: Antoine Parmentier made the potato popular in France.

125802.q: Which pathogen caused the great famine in Ireland from 1845?
125802.e: The water mould Phytophthora infestans causes late blight and destroyed several harvests. Ireland depended heavily on a few potato varieties.
125802.m: Late blight caused the Irish famine.

125803.q: Which poisonous substance builds up in green patches and sprouts of potatoes?
125803.e: Solanine is an alkaloid of the nightshade family. Green patches and sprouts should therefore be cut away generously.
125803.m: Green patches on potatoes contain poisonous solanine.

125804.q: Which pest introduced from North America eats the leaves of potato plants in Europe?
125804.e: The yellow and black striped Colorado potato beetle comes from North America and spread across Europe in the 20th century. Beetles and larvae can strip fields bare.
125804.m: The Colorado potato beetle is a pest introduced from North America.

125805.q: Why are potatoes in farming usually propagated from tubers rather than seeds?
a: The offspring are exactly like the variety
The plant does not form flowers
125805.e: Planting tubers produces genetically identical clones of the variety. That keeps the features the same, but makes whole fields vulnerable to the same diseases.
125805.m: Potatoes grown from tubers are clones of their mother plant.

125806.q: Where does the German word “Kartoffel” (potato) come from?
125806.e: The tubers reminded people of truffles, “tartufolo” in Italian. Via “Tartuffel”, this became the German word “Kartoffel”.
125806.m: The German word Kartoffel goes back to the Italian word for truffle.

125807.q: What is it called when a new behaviour is built up step by step by reinforcing closer and closer approximations?
125807.e: In shaping, every rough approximation of the target behaviour is rewarded at first, and then only more accurate ones. This is how Skinner taught animals complex sequences.
125807.m: In shaping, behaviour is formed through step-by-step reinforcement.

125808.e: Behaviourists treat the inner workings of a person as a “black box”. They study how stimuli and consequences shape visible behaviour.

125809.q: Which Russian physiologist discovered classical conditioning in dogs?
125809.e: Pavlov noticed that dogs started to salivate as soon as stimuli appeared that had regularly been paired with food. A neutral stimulus thus became a conditioned stimulus.
125809.m: Pavlov discovered classical conditioning in dogs.

125810.q: Which psychologist developed the theory of operant conditioning and an experimental box named after him?
125810.e: In his box, Skinner studied how rats and pigeons learn behaviour through rewards. Behaviour is controlled by its consequences.

125811.q: What does “negative reinforcement” mean in operant conditioning?
125811.e: With negative reinforcement, a behaviour becomes more frequent because it ends something unpleasant, such as fastening your seat belt to stop the warning beep in a car. It is not punishment.
125811.m: Negative reinforcement increases a behaviour by removing something unpleasant.

125812.q: Which controversial experiment from 1920 showed that fear can be conditioned in a small child?
125812.e: Watson and Rayner paired a white rat with a loud bang until the child showed fear even without the bang. Today the experiment is seen as ethically unacceptable.
125812.m: The Little Albert experiment conditioned fear in a small child.

125813.q: Which law did Edward Thorndike formulate using cats in puzzle boxes?
125813.e: According to the law of effect, behaviours with pleasant results are shown more often. This makes Thorndike a pioneer of operant conditioning.
125813.m: According to Thorndike, behaviour with pleasant results becomes more frequent.

125814.q: What is the gradual disappearance of a conditioned response called when reinforcement stops?
125814.e: If the conditioned stimulus is presented again and again without the unconditioned stimulus, the response weakens. However, it can later come back spontaneously.
125814.m: Without reinforcement, a learnt response dies out through extinction.

125815.q: Which linguist sharply criticised Skinner’s explanation of language learning in 1959?
125815.e: Chomsky argued that children form sentences they have never heard and do not learn language through reinforcement alone. His review is seen as an important push towards the cognitive revolution.
125815.m: Chomsky’s criticism of Skinner helped bring about the cognitive revolution.

125816.q: What does cognitive psychology deal with?
125816.e: Cognitive psychology studies the mental processes people use to take in, store and process information. These include attention, language and problem solving.
125816.m: Cognitive psychology studies thinking, perception and memory.

125817.q: Which school of thought, which only studied observable behaviour, did cognitive psychology distance itself from?
125817.e: Behaviourism refused to talk about inner processes. The cognitive revolution put thinking and memory back at the centre, and Ulric Neisser’s 1967 textbook gave the field its name.
125817.m: Cognitive psychology replaced behaviourism as the leading approach.

125818.q: Which image of the human mind did cognitive psychology shape?
a: A blank slate with no structure
125818.e: Taking the computer as a model, the mind was seen as a system that takes in, transforms and stores information. This view still shapes the field today.
125818.m: Cognitive psychology sees the mind as an information-processing system.

125819.q: Which memory model by Atkinson and Shiffrin distinguishes between sensory register, short-term memory and long-term memory?
125819.e: According to the multi-store model, information passes through the sensory register into short-term memory. Through repetition it is transferred into long-term memory.
125819.m: The multi-store model distinguishes three memory stores.

125820.q: What is it called when you miss an obvious event because your attention is focused on another task?
125820.e: In the famous gorilla experiment, participants count passes of a ball and often miss a person in a gorilla costume. So attention is highly selective.
125820.m: If you concentrate hard, you can easily miss the unexpected.

125821.q: Which psychologist received the Nobel Prize in Economics in 2002, partly for research on judgement heuristics?
125821.e: With Amos Tversky, Kahneman showed that people systematically depart from rationality when making decisions. Tversky had already died in 1996 and could not receive the prize.
125821.m: Daniel Kahneman showed that judgements follow systematic thinking errors.

125822.q: What is the effect called in which a number mentioned earlier influences later estimates?
125822.e: Even a random number can pull estimates in its direction. The anchoring effect is one of the best-known biases in judgement.
125822.m: In the anchoring effect, a starting number steers later estimates.

125823.q: What does the Stroop effect show?
a: Naming the colour of a colour word takes longer when they do not match
Pictures are forgotten faster than words
Reading something repeatedly wipes your memory
125823.e: If the word “red” is printed in blue, automatic reading gets in the way of naming the colour. The effect shows how hard it is to suppress automatic processes.
125823.m: In the Stroop effect, automatic reading interferes with naming the ink colour.

125824.q: Which model by Baddeley and Hitch describes a short-term system with a central executive and a phonological loop?
125824.e: Baddeley and Hitch replaced the single short-term store with several components that work together. The central executive controls attention.
125824.m: Working memory is made up of several components that work together.

125825.q: Which theory and method of treatment did Sigmund Freud found?
125825.e: Freud developed psychoanalysis as a theory of the unconscious and as a therapy. Patients were meant to become aware of unconscious conflicts by talking.

125826.q: In which city did Sigmund Freud live and work for most of his life?
125826.e: Freud lived in Vienna for decades, where a museum now remembers him. After Austria was annexed by Germany, he emigrated to London in 1938.
125826.m: Sigmund Freud worked mainly in Vienna.

125827.q: Which three parts of the mind does Freud distinguish in his structural model?
125827.e: The id stands for drives, the superego for internalised norms. The ego mediates between the two and reality.
125827.m: Freud’s structural model consists of id, ego and superego.

125828.q: Which work by Freud appeared around the turn of the century and interpreted dreams as a path to the unconscious?
a: Group Psychology and the Analysis of the Ego
125828.e: The book was delivered at the end of 1899 but bears the year 1900. Freud called the dream the “royal road” to the unconscious.
125828.m: In The Interpretation of Dreams, Freud saw dreams as a path to the unconscious.

125829.q: What is the psychoanalytic method called in which patients say everything that comes into their minds?
125829.e: The patients lie on the couch and are meant to say their thoughts without censoring them. This is meant to bring repressed content to the surface.
125829.m: In free association, you say whatever comes to mind without filtering it.

125830.q: What does Freud call the defence mechanism in which unpleasant content is kept out of consciousness?
125830.e: In repression, distressing thoughts or memories are pushed into the unconscious. Freud saw it as a central defence mechanism.
125830.m: Repression pushes distressing things into the unconscious.

125831.q: Which area of psychoanalysis did Freud’s daughter Anna Freud especially shape?
125831.e: Anna Freud worked mainly with children and developed the theory of defence mechanisms further. Her book “The Ego and the Mechanisms of Defence” appeared in 1936.

125832.q: How did Freud interpret slips of the tongue and other everyday mistakes?
a: As a sign of unconscious thoughts or wishes
As the result of tiredness with no meaning
As a sign of a brain disease
As the result of poor schooling
125832.e: Freud described mistakes such as slips of the tongue and forgetting in “The Psychopathology of Everyday Life”. Today people speak of a Freudian slip.
125832.m: A Freudian slip is said to reveal an unconscious thought.

125833.q: In which canton was Carl Gustav Jung born in 1875?
125833.e: Jung was born in Kesswil on Lake Constance and later grew up near Basel. He lived and worked mainly in Küsnacht on Lake Zurich.
125833.m: C. G. Jung was born in Thurgau.

125834.q: What did Carl Gustav Jung call his own school of psychology?
125834.e: After breaking with Freud, Jung called his approach analytical psychology. Individual psychology comes from Alfred Adler, logotherapy from Viktor Frankl.
125834.m: Jung’s school is called analytical psychology.

125835.q: According to Jung, which layer of the mind contains primordial images shared by all humans?
125835.e: Jung believed that beneath the personal unconscious lies a layer shared by all people. He said it shows itself in the myths, fairy tales and dreams of all cultures.
125835.m: The collective unconscious is shared by all humans.

125836.q: What does Jung call primordial images such as the “shadow” or the “wise old man” that appear in the myths of all cultures?
125836.e: According to Jung, archetypes are inborn patterns of experience and imagination. The shadow, for example, stands for the repressed, disliked sides of the personality.
125836.m: According to Jung, archetypes are universal primordial images.

125837.q: Which pair of personality terms did Carl Gustav Jung make well known?
125837.e: In “Psychological Types” from 1921, Jung described whether a person’s psychic energy is directed more inwards or outwards. The terms are now part of everyday language.
125837.m: Jung coined the terms introversion and extraversion.

125838.q: At which Zurich clinic did the young Jung work under Eugen Bleuler?
125838.e: At the Burghölzli in Zurich, Jung did research using, among other things, the word association experiment. Eugen Bleuler ran the clinic.
125838.m: Jung began his career at the Burghölzli clinic.

125839.q: What did Jung call the meaningful coming together in time of events with no causal connection?
125839.e: Jung meant events that are meaningfully connected for the person concerned, without one causing the other. The concept is scientifically disputed.
125839.m: Synchronicity means meaningful coincidences without a cause.

125840.q: Which psychoanalyst was Jung close friends with at first, before they fell out around 1913?
125840.e: For a time Freud saw Jung as his successor. Differing views on the unconscious and the drives led to their split.
125840.m: Jung and Freud split after years of close cooperation.

125841.q: What does Piaget call the tendency of preoperational children to pay attention to only one striking feature of a situation?
125841.e: A child might notice only the height of a column of water and overlook the width of the glass. Only with decentration can it take several features into account at once.
125841.m: Preoperational children often focus on only one feature.

125842.q: How many main stages of cognitive development does Jean Piaget distinguish?
125842.e: Piaget distinguishes the sensorimotor, the preoperational, the concrete operational and the formal operational stage. Each one builds on the one before.
125842.m: Piaget describes four stages of cognitive development.

125843.q: At which of Piaget’s stages does a young child acquire object permanence?
125843.e: In about the first two years of life, children learn that objects go on existing even when they cannot see them. Before that, they do not look for hidden things.
125843.m: Object permanence develops in the sensorimotor stage.

125844.q: Which feature of thinking does the three mountains task show in children at the preoperational stage?
125844.e: Children were asked how a doll on the other side would see a model of mountains. Younger children usually described their own view.
125844.m: Preoperational children find it hard to imagine other points of view.

125845.q: What do children at the concrete operational stage understand when water is poured into a narrower glass?
125845.e: From about the age of seven, children recognise the conservation of amounts despite a change in shape. Younger children are fooled by the taller column of water.
125845.m: Concrete operational children understand conservation of amounts.

125846.q: What does Piaget call fitting new experiences into an existing schema?
125846.e: A child who calls every four-legged animal “dog” fits new things into an existing schema. If the schema has to be changed, Piaget calls it accommodation.
125846.m: In assimilation, something new is fitted into an existing schema.

125847.q: According to Piaget, at roughly what age does the formal operational stage begin?
125847.e: At the formal operational stage, young people can think abstractly and hypothetically. They test assumptions systematically, even without concrete objects.
125847.m: According to Piaget, abstract thinking begins at about 11 to 12.

125848.q: In which Swiss city did Jean Piaget mainly do research and teach?
125848.e: Piaget was born in Neuchâtel and worked mainly at the University of Geneva. There he founded an international centre for the study of how knowledge develops.
125848.m: Jean Piaget did most of his research in Geneva.

125849.q: Which criticism does today’s research often make of Piaget’s stage model?
a: Children can do many things earlier than he thought
Children do not develop in stages at all
The model only applies to adults
125849.e: With simpler tasks, babies and toddlers show abilities that Piaget placed later. In addition, development happens in fewer sudden jumps than was thought.
125849.m: Children show many abilities earlier than Piaget thought.

125850.q: What did Stanley Milgram study with his experiment from 1961?
125850.e: Milgram wanted to know how far people would go when an authority told them to do harmful things. The experiment became one of the best known in social psychology.
125850.m: The Milgram experiment studied obedience to authority.

125851.q: At which university did Stanley Milgram carry out his obedience experiment?
125851.e: The experiments took place at Yale University in the USA. In later versions, Milgram moved the location to test the influence of prestige.
125851.m: Milgram carried out his experiments at Yale University.

125852.q: Which historical event gave Milgram the idea for his studies of obedience?
a: The building of the Berlin Wall
125852.e: Milgram asked whether those who carried out the Holocaust had simply obeyed orders. The Eichmann trial in Jerusalem began in 1961, the same year as his experiments.
125852.m: The Eichmann trial inspired Milgram’s studies.

125853.q: What role did the “learner” in the Milgram experiment really play?
a: He was an actor who was in on it
He was a randomly chosen person
125853.e: The learner received no real electric shocks but acted out cries of pain. The real participants were the “teachers”.
125853.m: In the Milgram experiment, nobody was really shocked.

125854.q: How many participants in the basic version went on to the strongest supposed electric shock?
125854.e: In the best-known version, about 65 per cent of the “teachers” gave the highest shock of 450 volts. Beforehand, experts had expected only very few people to do so.
125854.m: In Milgram’s basic version, about two thirds obeyed to the end.

125855.q: Which change clearly reduced obedience in Milgram’s versions?
a: An experimenter in a white coat
125855.e: When the teachers had to be in the same room or press the learner’s hand onto the plate, far fewer obeyed. The experimenter being absent also reduced obedience.
125855.m: The closer the victim was, the less the participants obeyed.

125856.q: How did Milgram explain why so many participants obeyed to the end?
a: They shifted the responsibility onto the experimenter
They deliberately wanted to harm the learner
125856.e: Milgram spoke of the agentic state: people then see themselves only as a tool of an authority. They pass the responsibility for their actions on to that authority.
125856.m: If you see yourself as a tool of an authority, you no longer feel responsible yourself.

125857.q: Why is the Milgram experiment now seen as ethically problematic?
a: The participants were deceived and put under great strain
The participants received real electric shocks
The participants were all under age
The participants knew everything in advance
125857.e: Many participants trembled, sweated or laughed nervously because they believed they were hurting someone. Today’s ethical guidelines no longer allow such experiments in this form.
125857.m: Deception and great strain make the Milgram experiment ethically controversial.

125858.q: Which psychologist led the Stanford Prison Experiment in 1971?
125858.e: Philip Zimbardo had students play the roles of guards and prisoners in a mock prison. He himself took the role of prison superintendent.
125858.m: Philip Zimbardo led the Stanford Prison Experiment.

125859.q: Where was the prison for the Stanford Prison Experiment set up?
a: In the basement of the psychology building
125859.e: A corridor in the basement of the psychology department at Stanford University was turned into cells. The prisoners had first been picked up at home by real police officers.
125859.m: The Stanford prison was in the university basement.

125860.q: How were the roles of guards and prisoners given out?
125860.e: A coin toss decided the role of the students, who had first been judged to be ordinary. This was so that differences would come from the situation and not from personality.
125860.m: The roles in the Stanford Prison Experiment were given out at random.

125861.q: After how many days was the experiment, planned for two weeks, stopped?
125861.e: The situation quickly got out of hand, and several prisoners showed severe stress reactions. Zimbardo ended the experiment early.
125861.m: The Stanford Prison Experiment ended after only six days.

125862.q: Why is the Stanford Prison Experiment now considered ethically unacceptable?
a: The participants suffered serious psychological strain
It was carried out without a university
125862.e: Several prisoners showed severe stress reactions, and those running the experiment stepped in too late. Today ethics committees have to check such experiments beforehand.
125862.m: The Stanford Prison Experiment failed to protect its participants.

125863.q: What main objection is made today to the value of the Stanford Prison Experiment as evidence?
a: The guards were encouraged to behave harshly
The experiment lasted far too long
125863.e: Later analyses of archive material showed that the people running it urged the guards to be tough. This makes it doubtful whether the behaviour came from the role alone.
125863.m: The guards in the Stanford experiment were coached in their behaviour.

125864.q: What was the Stanford Prison Experiment originally meant to show?
a: How strongly a role and a situation shape behaviour
How long people can go without sleep
Whether prisons can be built more cheaply
125864.e: Zimbardo wanted to find out whether ordinary people change a lot in the role of guard or prisoner. Later the way it was carried out was criticised.
125864.m: The experiment was meant to show the power of the situation.

125865.q: What is the title of Zimbardo’s book in which he compares Stanford with the abuse at Abu Ghraib prison?
a: Eichmann in Jerusalem: A Report on the Banality of Evil
125865.e: Zimbardo argued that situations can lead ordinary people to commit cruel acts. He also appeared as an expert witness about Abu Ghraib.
125865.m: In The Lucifer Effect, Zimbardo stresses the power of the situation.

125866.q: Who developed the theory of cognitive dissonance in 1957?
125866.e: Leon Festinger described dissonance as an unpleasant tension between conflicting thoughts, attitudes or actions. People try to reduce this tension.
125866.m: Leon Festinger founded the theory of cognitive dissonance.

125867.q: What is meant by cognitive dissonance?
a: Tension caused by thoughts or actions that do not fit together
Joy about an expectation coming true
125867.e: Someone who smokes and knows smoking is harmful, for example, experiences an inner contradiction. This tension motivates them to change their attitude or behaviour.
125867.m: Cognitive dissonance is a tension between cognitions that do not fit together.

125868.q: In the experiment by Festinger and Carlsmith (1959), which group rated a boring task most positively?
a: Those who were paid one dollar for lying
Those who were paid twenty dollars for lying
Those who did not have to lie at all
Those who were punished for lying
125868.e: With only one dollar, there was no outside justification for the lie. So the participants changed their attitude and found the task more interesting.
125868.m: A small reward led to a bigger change of attitude.

125869.q: Which fable by Aesop is seen as a classic example of reducing cognitive dissonance?
125869.e: The fox cannot reach the grapes and so declares that they are sour. In this way he changes his judgement instead of admitting failure.
125869.m: The fox declares the grapes he cannot reach to be sour.

125870.q: What is often seen after a difficult decision between two alternatives?
a: The chosen option is rated more highly
The chosen option is rated lower
Both options are rated the same
125870.e: After choosing, people stress the advantages of the chosen option and the disadvantages of the rejected one. In this way they reduce post-decision dissonance.
125870.m: After a decision, people usually rate the chosen option more highly.

125871.q: Which book by Festinger and colleagues describes a group whose prophecy of the end of the world did not come true?
125871.e: Instead of giving up, many members campaigned even harder for their belief after the disaster failed to happen. Festinger interpreted this as a way of reducing dissonance.
125871.m: After a failed prophecy, believers strengthened their faith.

125872.q: Which strategy does NOT help to reduce cognitive dissonance?
a: Adding new thoughts that justify it
125872.e: Dissonance is reduced by changing one of the conflicting cognitions or adding supporting thoughts. Stressing the contradiction would increase the tension.
125872.m: Dissonance is reduced by adjusting attitudes, behaviour or justifications.

125873.q: What is the tendency called to look mainly for information that confirms your own opinion?
125873.e: Anyone who avoids contradicting information protects themselves from dissonance. This selective search for information is a well-documented thinking error.
125873.m: Confirmation bias makes us prefer information that fits.

125874.q: What does the “O” in the Big Five acronym OCEAN stand for?
125874.e: OCEAN stands for openness, conscientiousness, extraversion, agreeableness and neuroticism. Openness describes curiosity, imagination and interest in new things.
125874.m: The O in OCEAN stands for openness to experience.

125875.q: Which of the following traits is NOT one of the Big Five?
125875.e: The Big Five are openness, conscientiousness, extraversion, agreeableness and neuroticism. Intelligence is measured as a separate area.
125875.m: Intelligence is not one of the five big personality factors.

125876.q: Which Big Five dimension describes a tendency towards anxiety, irritability and emotional instability?
125876.e: People with high neuroticism experience negative feelings and stress more often. The opposite pole is called emotional stability.

125877.q: Which basic idea is the lexical approach, from which the Big Five came, based on?
a: Important traits are rooted in language
Traits can be read from the skull
Personality depends on your star sign
125877.e: Researchers collected words for traits from dictionaries and analysed them statistically. This revealed five big factors.
125877.m: The lexical approach looks for personality traits in language.

125878.q: Which statistical method was used to obtain the five factors from many trait descriptions?
125878.e: Factor analysis groups closely related traits into a few higher-level factors. With personality words, five factors appeared again and again.
125878.m: The Big Five were found using factor analysis.

125879.q: Which Big Five dimension usually best predicts performance at school and at work?
125879.e: Conscientious people are organised, reliable and persistent. Many studies show links with marks and job performance.
125879.m: Conscientiousness is most strongly linked to performance.

125880.q: How do Big Five scores change on average during adulthood?
a: All scores stay the same from birth
Openness rises sharply into old age
125880.e: This pattern is called the maturity principle. At the same time, neuroticism falls slightly on average.
125880.m: With age, people become more conscientious and agreeable on average.

125881.q: Which personality model adds the factor honesty-humility to the Big Five?
125881.e: The HEXACO model has six factors. The extra factor describes fairness, sincerity and modesty.
125881.m: The HEXACO model has six personality factors.

125882.q: How are the Big Five traits described, unlike type models?
125882.e: Everyone has a score somewhere between two poles on each of the five dimensions. Most people are in the middle range.
125882.m: The Big Five are continuous dimensions, not types.

125883.q: In which city was Hermann Rorschach born in 1884?
125883.e: Rorschach was born in Zurich and grew up in Schaffhausen. He studied medicine and became a psychiatrist.
125883.m: Hermann Rorschach was born in Zurich.

125884.q: How many cards does the Rorschach test have?
125884.e: The test consists of ten cards with symmetrical inkblots, some black and grey, some coloured. The person being tested describes what they see in them.
125884.m: The Rorschach test has ten cards.

125885.q: What kind of psychological test is the Rorschach test?
125885.e: In projective tests, people are asked to interpret ambiguous material. It is assumed that they reveal their own patterns of thinking and feeling as they do so.
125885.m: The Rorschach test is a projective method.

125886.q: What is the person being tested asked to do in the Rorschach test?
a: Describe what they recognise in inkblots
Do sums as fast as possible
125886.e: The person interprets symmetrical inkblots. Conclusions about their thinking and feelings are meant to be drawn from the answers.
125886.m: In the Rorschach test, you interpret inkblots.

125887.e: Rorschach studied medicine and worked as a psychiatrist, finally at the clinic in Herisau. There he developed his inkblot test.

125888.q: What was Hermann Rorschach’s nickname at school?
125888.e: Rorschach liked drawing, and playing with inkblot pictures was popular at the time. The nickname, German for “blot”, fits his later test remarkably well.
125888.m: Even as a schoolboy, Rorschach was called “Klecks”, meaning “blot”.

125889.q: Roughly how old was Hermann Rorschach when he died in 1922?
125889.e: Rorschach died unexpectedly in 1922 of peritonitis. He was only 37 years old.

125890.q: What main objection do critics raise against the Rorschach test?
a: Doubts about its reliability and validity
It takes too long for children
The cards are free of copyright
125890.e: Different assessors sometimes reach different results, and many interpretations are poorly supported. Standardised scoring systems were meant to reduce these weaknesses.
125890.m: The scientific quality of the Rorschach test is the main thing in doubt.

125891.q: Which psychologist developed the marshmallow test?
125891.e: Walter Mischel carried out the experiments around 1970 at a preschool at Stanford University. Later he followed the children for decades.
125891.m: Walter Mischel developed the marshmallow test.

125892.q: What choice were the children given in the classic marshmallow test?
a: One sweet now or two later
Two sweets now or one later
One sweet or a small toy
Play now or tidy up first
125892.e: The experimenter left the room; anyone who waited until he came back got a second sweet. Anyone who rang the bell or ate before then got only one.
125892.m: In the marshmallow test, waiting paid off with a double reward.

125893.q: Which strategy especially helped children in the marshmallow test to wait longer?
a: Holding the sweet in their hand
125893.e: Children who sang, closed their eyes or imagined the sweet as a picture held out longer. Focusing on its tempting features made them wait less long.
125893.m: Distraction helps you put off a reward.

125894.q: Which link was reported in Mischel’s follow-up studies?
a: Waiting longer went along with better later achievements
Waiting longer led to worse marks
There were no follow-up studies at all
Waiting time depended only on height
125894.e: Children who waited longer did better years later, for example in college entrance tests. However, the sample was small and not very varied.
125894.m: Mischel’s follow-up studies found links with later achievements.

125895.q: What did a large replication study of the marshmallow test in 2018 find?
a: The link was weaker and depended on family background
The original results were much stronger
Children no longer wait at all today
125895.e: When the parents’ education and income were taken into account, the predictive value shrank a lot. Self-control alone explained later achievements only a little.
125895.m: Newer studies put the marshmallow test’s significance into perspective.

125896.q: What did a version show in which the experimenter had broken promises beforehand?
a: The children waited much less long
The children were no longer given a choice
125896.e: If children had found that the adult was unreliable, grabbing the sweet straight away was a sensible decision. So waiting also depends on trust.
125896.m: Children wait longer if they can trust the adult.

125897.q: Mischel distinguished an impulsive and a thoughtful system in the mind. Which one must win for a child to be able to wait for the reward?
125897.e: The hot system reacts quickly to tempting stimuli, while the cool system plans and thinks about the consequences. Self-control works when the cool system holds back the hot one.
125897.m: Self-control comes when the cool system holds back the hot system.

125898.q: What did Walter Mischel show in 1968 about personality and behaviour?
a: The situation often influences behaviour more strongly than fixed traits
Behaviour is determined by genes alone
Behaviour can be read from handwriting
125898.e: In his book “Personality and Assessment”, Mischel showed that traits such as honesty only weakly predict behaviour in individual situations. This started the person-situation debate.
125898.m: The situation also determines how we behave.

125899.q: Which psychologist presented a hierarchy of human needs in 1943?
125899.e: Abraham Maslow published his theory of motivation in the essay “A Theory of Human Motivation”. It is often shown as a pyramid.
125899.m: Abraham Maslow arranged needs in a hierarchy.

125900.q: In Maslow’s model, which level of needs comes directly after the basic physical needs?
125900.e: After food, water and sleep, people seek protection, order and stability. Only after that do belonging and recognition become important.
125900.m: In Maslow’s model, safety comes after the basic needs.

125901.q: Which basic assumption lies behind the order in Maslow’s hierarchy?
a: Higher needs only become important after lower ones
All needs are always equally important
Higher needs must be met first
The order changes randomly every day
125901.e: According to Maslow, unmet lower needs dominate behaviour. Only when they are largely met do higher needs come to the fore.
125901.m: In Maslow’s model, lower needs take priority.

125902.q: What does Maslow call the needs of the lower levels, whose absence causes restlessness?
125902.e: Deficiency needs lose their driving force once they are met. Growth needs such as self-actualisation, on the other hand, can never be fully satisfied.
125902.m: Deficiency needs only drive us while they are unmet.

125903.q: Which school of psychology does Abraham Maslow belong to?
125903.e: Humanistic psychology stresses growth, self-determination and human potential. It is often called the “third force” alongside psychoanalysis and behaviourism.

125904.q: Which level is at the very top of the well-known picture of Maslow’s hierarchy of needs?
125904.e: The well-known pyramid ends with self-actualisation, the drive to develop your own abilities. In late writings, Maslow also added self-transcendence.
125904.m: Self-actualisation is at the top of Maslow’s pyramid.

125905.q: Which criticism is often made of Maslow’s hierarchy of needs?
a: The order of levels is not strictly supported by evidence
It has too many levels to be practical
It only applies to animals, not humans
125905.e: People often pursue several needs at the same time, even when lower ones are not met. In addition, the order reflects individualistic cultures more than others.
125905.m: The strict order of Maslow’s pyramid is disputed.

125906.q: Who drew the well-known pyramid shape of the hierarchy of needs?
125906.e: There is no pyramid in Maslow’s original texts. The picture became popular later, especially in management textbooks.
125906.m: Maslow’s pyramid was not drawn by Maslow himself.

125907.q: Where do you stick the AED pads on adults in the standard position?
a: Below the right collarbone and on the left side of the chest
Both pads next to each other on the breastbone
One on the stomach and one on the lower back
One pad on each upper arm
125907.e: This way the current flows diagonally through the heart. The devices also show the position on the pads with a picture.
125907.m: The AED pads place the heart between them.

125908.q: In ventricular fibrillation without defibrillation, roughly how does the chance of survival change per minute?
a: It falls by about 7 to 10 per cent
